item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Clarke Schmidt to see doctor amid new injury concerns appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees' bid for the AL East crown may be all but lost, as they sit six games behind division-leader Tampa Bay Rays in the standings with seven games remaining in the regular season, but the important thing is that they have secured a spot in the Wild Card round — marking their 27th postseason berth in 34 seasons (they are currently in the middle of a 34-year winning season streak).
The key now for the Yankees is keeping their key players healthy. While the Yankees have been mostly healthy on the pitching side of things, reliever Clarke Schmidt, who returned to big-league action on September 16 after a lengthy layoff, suffered some bicep cramping on Sunday, which then prevented him from suiting up in their 8-4 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks.
While Bob Nightengale of USA Today reported that Schmidt's inability to show up on the mound was merely precautionary, he will be meeting with a doctor back in New York to ascertain that he's not suffering from any underlying serious injury that could keep him out for an extended period once more.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Schmidt didn't make his 2026 season debut until September after he underwent elbow surgery (internal brace procedure), so at least he's not suffering any setbacks in that regard.
The 30-year-old righty struck out two in 0.2 innings of work in his only appearance of 2026 in a 5-4 loss for the Yankees against the Minnesota Twins.
The Yankees have already been dealt a huge injury blow, with Aaron Judge, who only recently returned to action, suffering a calf strain that sent him back to the injured list. They already have Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham among lineup regulars already on the IL.
While New York has enough depth to make up for the absences of a few players, they would want to enter the postseason as close to full strength as they can get. With the Wild Card round set to begin in nine days, they have some time to get it together from a health standpoint.
Related: Yankees' Spencer Jones shuts down injury concern ahead of postseason

item.title: [Newsday] Erik Boland: Yankees' upcoming week all about Aaron Judge
item.dc:creator: Erik Boland

item.content:encoded:
A 3-3 road trip at this point of the long season for almost any big-league team would be considered at least a minor success.
The 3-3 trip for the Yankees that concluded with Sunday’s 8-4 loss to the Diamondbacks was nothing short of disastrous.
And potentially season-altering — and not in a good way — depending on the prognosis for Aaron Judge’s right calf.
It all starts there, of course.
This time it was something other than Judge’s upper body commanding attention. During the previous three months-plus, he battled his way back from a right rib stress fracture, missing 84 games.
In the early innings of Wednesday’s loss to the Twins in Minneapolis, Judge felt discomfort in his right calf. He eventually gave way to a pinch hitter in the top of the sixth inning of what turned into a 5-4, 13-inning loss.
That defeat all but put an end to the Yankees’ AL East title hopes. They fell 4 1⁄2 games behind the Rays on Wednesday and now are six back with seven games to play. The Rays’ magic number is down to two, which means that if the Yankees lose even one of the four games against Tampa Bay this week, the division race is over.
So the 3-3 trip essentially cemented the Yankees as a wild-card team and sucked any remaining drama there might have been for this week’s series at the Stadium. The Yankees are a club headed for a best-of-three Wild Card Series showdown with the Red Sox.
Winning three of four against the Red Sox from Aug. 28-30 and outscoring them 26-9 gave the Yankees a 7-6 edge in the season series.
A Yankees-Red Sox matchup at the Stadium in the wild-card round has seemed fairly inevitable since Boston left town the night of Aug. 30 after a 16-1 loss.
As incredible as the Red Sox’s 32-5 stretch was, they have gone 52-67 the rest of the season. They cut the Yankees’ 15 1⁄2-game lead to a half-game with that hot streak but never caught them, and they have gone 20-21 since the streak ended on Aug. 7.
So before the road trip to Minnesota and Arizona, the potential of a wild-card matchup with the Red Sox — aside from the anything-can-happen element that goes with any short series in baseball — hadn’t thrown a huge scare into the fan base.
Now, however, Judge seems questionable at best for that series, which has taken on a far different look — and created additional angst for Yankees fans — with the potential of the three-time American League MVP missing it entirely or being severely limited in it.
While it’s true the Yankees managed that season-series win against the Red Sox without Judge, who did not return until Sept. 8, that late August series was mostly an outlier when it came to the performance of their offense when the outfielder was out.
The Yankees did well enough in Judge’s absence with a more than respectable 45-39 record, but the difference in the offense’s numbers were striking.
Through May 31, the last game Judge played before going on the injured list in early June, Yankees were 36-23, averaging 5.2 runs per game and hitting .243 with a .770 OPS.
Without Judge before his return on Sept. 8? The offense averaged 4.1 runs per game and hit .227 with a .681 OPS in that 45-39 stretch.
The upcoming week now becomes all about Judge. The only question that matters: Just how serious is his calf strain?
In the least surprising development that has occurred since Judge came out of Wednesday’s game, the Yankees, taking their cue from the outfielder, have said little regarding what’s to come.
But even within the vagueness of most of the answers, there was room for tea-leaf reading.
A somber Aaron Boone said after Wednesday’s game (before knowing of the upcoming MRI tests): “Hopefully we get it treated and knock it out and he’ll be a factor at some point.”
The “some point” sent up all kinds of red flags.
Judge, speaking to reporters in Phoenix on Saturday, said, “I’d like to be back by the postseason. That’s definitely the plan.”
Judge saying he’d “like” to be back by the playoffs — which for the Yankees are very likely to begin Sept. 29 — and that doing so is “the plan” is not the same as a “this is a small thing; I’ll be back” guarantee.
That Judge, who did not play in any rehab games before his return, went 4-for-23 with 13 strikeouts and one homer in seven games before returning to the injured list is not relevant.
It’s his mere presence in the lineup — and what it represents in terror factor to opposing pitchers, regardless of whether Judge is in a hot streak or cold streak — that matters.
What kind of a presence Judge will be come Sept. 29 — and whether he will be a presence at all — will take center stage in evaluating the week to come, and not how the Yankees do against the Rays and Orioles to end the season.
Judge’s calf is now all that matters this week, a week that, up until this 3-3 trip, appeared assured of meaning so much more.

item.title: [MLB.com] 1 player to watch on each team during final week of season
item.dc:creator: MLB com

item.content:encoded:
There’s a lot on the line before the 2026 regular season wraps up on Sunday, including postseason seeding, statistical milestones and player development. And even for the players and teams who won’t be chasing a World Series title, finishing the season strong is always important.
With the help of MLB.com’s beat writers, here is one player to watch on each team during the final week of the regular season.
American League East
Blue Jays: 1B Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Over and over again, the flashes we’ve seen from Guerrero have fizzled. He was the face of the Blue Jays’ run to Game 7 of the World Series a year ago, but now, he’s the face of their disappointing 2026. It’s still so easy to believe in Guerrero when you see these flashes of his incredible talent, but he’s hit just nine home runs this season and has been living with an OPS under .700, stunning numbers for someone of his stature. Still, he’s the player with the most power to change this team’s trajectory, and if anyone can help salvage this season, it’s Guerrero. -- Keegan Matheson
Orioles: 1B Pete Alonso
Who else? If the O’s are going to make an improbable push into the postseason as a Wild Card team, it will likely be because of Alonso, who has done everything in his power to keep his team in the race down the stretch. There have been only nine 40-plus-homer seasons in Orioles history (since 1954), but Alonso could join the list with a strong finish to his first campaign in Baltimore. -- Jake Rill
Rays: 3B Junior Caminero
With all due respect to Chandler Simpson’s bid for both the AL batting crown and stolen-base title, this one’s pretty simple. Caminero has established himself as a legitimate candidate for the AL MVP Award alongside Yordan Alvarez. He’s leading the AL in home runs. He’s tracking toward starting all 162 games at third base. He’s the best player on the best team in the AL. And as an opening act for his first real moment in the postseason spotlight, he hit the first two walk-off homers of his career -- including one to clinch a playoff berth. Caminero’s power and energy always make him a player to watch, and that’s especially true as the Rays work to lock down their first division title since 2021. -- Adam Berry
Red Sox: LHP Garrett Crochet
The ace lefty is in a race against time to help the Red Sox as a reliever by the Wild Card round of the playoffs. Here is what's on the docket for Crochet: at least one live batting practice session at Fenway Park early in the week. After that, he would likely throw another live BP or a simulated game. An outside possibility would be the Red Sox getting him a tune-up in a regular-season game. Crochet last pitched for the Sox on April 25 before going down with a left shoulder injury. Most players wouldn’t go cold turkey into the playoffs after not pitching for so long, but Crochet has the chance to make the type of impact that could make it worthwhile. -- Ian Browne
Yankees: RHP Cam Schlittler
No matter where you stand on the issue of a pitcher winning the MVP Award, there’s no debating that Schlittler has earned that title within the Yankees’ clubhouse, putting the finishing touches on the club’s best pitching season since Ron Guidry in 1978. Those Yankees won a championship, and now the current group will lean on the 25-year-old from Walpole, Mass., to lead them toward the Canyon of Heroes for the first time since 2009. -- Bryan Hoch
AL Central
Guardians: 3B José Ramírez
Ramírez has produced below his superstar standard this season, in which he has dealt with the aftereffects of left hamate surgery he underwent in June. It’s something he’ll have to manage the remainder of 2026, but the 34-year-old might be turning it on at the right time. Ramírez is 8-for-17 with three doubles, one home run and three RBIs in his past four games. -- Tim Stebbins
Royals: C Carter Jensen
Jensen’s breakout rookie season has cemented him alongside Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone as a core piece for a club looking to compete again in 2027. He’s already set Royals rookie records for home runs (25) and extra-base hits (60). Oh, and he’s done it while batting leadoff (he holds another record there, too) and taking over everyday catching duties from Salvador Perez. -- Jackson Stone
Tigers: SS/3B Kevin McGonigle
This could be the week that McGonigle wraps up the AL Rookie of the Year race. He’s the first rookie since Aaron Judge in 2017, and the fifth since 1990, to reach base safely 256 times in a season. He has more walks (94) than strikeouts (92) and is just the fifth rookie in the Divisional Era (since 1969) with that many walks in a season. And he joins Ted Williams as the only rookies in history to post at least 95 runs, 26 doubles, 17 homers, 70 RBIs and 93 walks. He has a chance to lead all AL position players in Baseball-Reference WAR, entering Sunday atop the AL at 6.8. -- Jason Beck
Twins: OF Emmanuel Rodriguez
Rodriguez has already shown his all-around skill set, from power to plate discipline to speed and defense. The only thing that has held him back over his pro career has been health, and now that he’s on the field, he’s hard to take your eyes off. Rodriguez is one of a slew of young Twins trying to cement their spots on the 2027 roster. -- Courtney Hollmon
White Sox: 1B Munetaka Murakami
Right-handed reliever Mike Vasil, also known as the Windy City Wizard for his dugout wand magic, said it best about Murakami: When he goes, the team goes. Murakami changed this franchise upon his arrival from Japan, taking the focus off a 6-13 team start and putting it upon his strong exploits on the field. Murakami has struggled since the start of August but showed his importance via a mammoth three-run home run in the first inning of a 3-1 victory over Detroit on Thursday. If Murakami can get hot over these final two series, the White Sox could punch their unexpected playoff ticket. -- Scott Merkin
AL West
Angels: C/1B/DH Moisés Ballesteros
Ballesteros got off to a slow start after being acquired in a trade that sent reliever Ryan Zeferjahn to the Cubs at the Trade Deadline but has been heating up offensively in September. He’s also been faring better than expected defensively at both catcher and first base. The 22-year-old was ranked as a Top 100 prospect by MLB Pipeline before each of the last two seasons, and the Angels would love to see him develop into a much-needed power bat from the left side. -- Rhett Bollinger
Astros: DH Yordan Alvarez
Shortstop Jeremy Peña said it best Thursday: “Obviously, Yordan is our horse.” After a 35-game stretch (Aug. 3-Sept. 13) in which he slashed .242/.380/.383 with three homers (since Aug. 3) to loosen his grip on the AL MVP Award, Alvarez homered in two of three games against the Royals last week and is still in contention for the Triple Crown. Alvarez leads the AL in batting average (.313) and is second in homers (40) and RBIs (99). -- Brian McTaggart 
Athletics: OF Henry Bolte
The A’s saw a five-tool talent in Bolte when they drafted him out of high school in 2022, and that has played out this year as he’s become just the third rookie in franchise history with at least 10 home runs and 20 stolen bases in a season and the first since Mitchell Page in 1977. Still just scratching the surface of his abilities, Bolte is building for what could be true star potential from him in 2027. -- Martín Gallegos
Mariners: INF/OF Michael Arroyo
Seattle's No. 3 prospect and MLB Pipeline's No. 42 overall prospect has played sparingly -- just five starts in the team’s 13 games since he made his MLB debut on Sept. 6. But that's been primarily due to a lack of positional runway. He came up as a second baseman but has transitioned more to left field this season. However, both those spots are occupied (by Cole Young and Randy Arozarena, respectively). Arroyo is a big part of the club's longer-term plans and has shown what he can do with the bat. How he's used in this final week could be a springboard for 2027. -- Daniel Kramer
Rangers: SS Corey Seager
Seager is the engine that keeps the Rangers offense going, and his absence has been felt throughout his three separate stints on the injured list this season (twice with back issues, once with a concussion). As he played sporadically in the first half, Seager hit just .182/.292/.374 as he battled injuries. Since returning from his last IL stint on July 31, he’s hitting .285 with an .837 OPS and eight homers in 45 games. The Rangers will only go as far as Seager takes them. And lately, he looks like the player who can put the team on his back. -- Kennedi Landry
National League East
Braves: RHP Robert Suarez
Suarez made a rehab appearance on Sunday with Triple-A Gwinnett, striking out one in a scoreless inning. The veteran reliever hasn’t pitched in the Majors since he was shut down in late June with a 0.56 ERA. There’s hope he will pitch in a big league game before the postseason begins, but the Braves haven’t committed to activating him before the regular season concludes. -- Mark Bowman
Marlins: SS Otto Lopez
A 2026 All-Star, Lopez needs 15 hits over his final six games to become the first Marlin since Luis Arraez in 2023 to reach 200 hits. Lopez (.305) trails Arraez (.313) and D-backs catcher Gabriel Moreno (.307) for the National League batting title. If Lopez can somehow leapfrog that pair, he would be the fourth NL batting champion in franchise history, joining Arraez ('23), Dee Strange-Gordon ('15) and Hanley Ramirez ('09). -- Christina De Nicola
Mets: RHP Jonah Tong
Few Mets players have as much to prove as Tong, who spent most of this season in the Minors before recently returning and flashing some much-improved form. If Tong can finish the year with another solid start, he will position himself well for what’s sure to be a lively rotation competition next spring. If he falters, he’ll only give the Mets more reason to be wary of him. -- Anthony DiComo
Nationals: OF James Wood
Wood slugged his way into his second All-Star selection, then missed 27 games because of a left oblique strain. He returned from the IL on Sept. 2 and is batting .259 with a .698 OPS this month. Wood, who just turned 24 on Thursday, will look to make up for the time he lost to injury and close out the final week of the season strong. -- Jessica Camerato
Phillies: LHP Jesús Luzardo
Luzardo is on the 15-day injured list with inflammation in his left shoulder. He’s eligible to be activated on Sunday, the final game of the regular season. It doesn’t necessarily matter if he pitches or not that day. It matters if the Phillies think Luzardo, who began throwing on Sunday, can pitch in the NL Wild Card Series, which begins on Sept. 29. If he can pitch, can he start? Or does he come out of the bullpen? He’s been arguably baseball’s best pitcher for months, so the Phillies need him one way or another. -- Todd Zolecki
NL Central
Brewers: RHP Jacob Misiorowski
Misiorowski probably has the National League Cy Young Award locked up. And his final regular-season start later this week will probably be tapered, since there’s no need to push his pitch count into dangerous territory. But the outing is still important, because it offers the Brewers’ young ace one final opportunity to build confidence going into what will surely be a Game 1 start in the NL Division Series. No club better showcases the fact that baseball is a team sport, but there’s little doubt that Misiorowski is singularly important to Milwaukee’s October hopes. -- Adam McCalvy
Cardinals: 1B Alec Burleson
Outfielder Jordan Walker received a lot of publicity because of his breakout season and winning the T-Mobile Home Run Derby, but Burleson is the man on the Cardinals, currently leading the Major Leagues with 111 RBIs. The last Cardinal to lead the big leagues in that department was Joe Torre (137) in 1971, and the last to lead the National League was Albert Pujols (118) in 2010. Burleson also leads the Majors with 61 hits with runners in scoring position, the most by a Cardinal since Brian Jordan (62) in 1996. -- Bill Ladson
Cubs: OF Pete Crow-Armstrong
All the “P-C-A” chants at Wrigley Field have transformed into “M-V-P” chants every time Crow-Armstrong steps to the plate for the North Siders. Crow-Armstrong is vying to become just the seventh player in MLB history to finish with at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases. Beyond keeping an eye on how high he can get those numbers, Cubs fans want to see just how high Crow-Armstrong’s MLB-leading WAR (10.5, per FanGraphs) can get before season’s end. And then, of course, the question will be whether the star center fielder can play like an MVP in October. -- Jordan Bastian
Pirates: SS Konnor Griffin
Pittsburgh fans have received small samples of what Griffin can do as baseball’s former top prospect. After missing most of the summer due to two separate IL stints, Griffin has become a regular at shortstop and in the leadoff spot to finish out his rookie campaign. To put it simply, Griffin is both the present and the future. Keep a close eye on his continued ascension in the final week. -- Aiden Stepansky
Reds: 1B Sal Stewart
Stewart will be trying to put the finishing touches on a season that should net him the NL Rookie of the Year Award. The 22-year-old is the 14th rookie since 1920 to post a 30-homer, 100-RBI season, and each of the last nine that did it since the award started in 1947 have won it, the most recent being Pete Alonso for the Mets in 2019. Stewart is currently second in MLB overall in RBIs with 110. If he can overtake Burleson, he would be the third rookie to finish a season leading in that category since RBIs became an official statistic in 1913, joining Ted Williams (1939) and Walt Dropo (1950). -- Mark Sheldon
NL West
D-backs: OF Corbin Carroll
Carroll battled a lower back issue which clearly hampered him at the plate, but after taking a couple of days off to rest, he has begun to swing the bat much better. As the D-backs have seen many times in the past when Carroll gets hot, it’s something to see. If they get his bat going and Gabriel Moreno and Nolan Arenado continue to swing it the way they have, the D-backs will have a puncher’s chance during the final week. -- Steve Gilbert
Dodgers: TWP Shohei Ohtani
Ohtani landed on the 15-day IL for the first time as a Dodger when his ongoing right biceps and left knee issues lingered into the beginning of September. He is done for the season as a pitcher, but he's expected back as a hitter. The final week of the regular season will be important for Ohtani, whether he returns in time to play a few games or tunes up his swing behind the scenes. -- Sonja Chen
Giants: 1B Bryce Eldridge
Now that Rafael Devers is out for the season, Eldridge -- once he clears concussion protocol --  has the chance to play first base every day for the Giants. The 21-year-old rookie has made some impressive strides with his defense, but his calling card remains his big bat, which has produced several majestic homers this year, including a 461-foot blast on Tuesday night at Busch Stadium. The Giants have struggled to develop star hitters in recent years, but Eldridge’s tantalizing power should give them plenty to dream on heading into 2027. -- Maria Guardado
Padres: RHP Nick Pivetta
Pivetta missed nearly five months with a flexor strain in his right elbow. His first few starts since returning have been mostly solid. The Padres have serious rotation questions heading into the postseason and will be assessing Pivetta’s final outing with a keen eye on what kind of usage might lie ahead for him in October. If they can get the dominant version of Pivetta that finished sixth in NL Cy Young voting last season, it would go a long way. -- AJ Cassavell
Rockies: 1B TJ Rumfield
Blocked in the Yankees organization, Rumfield flourished after being acquired in a quiet deal last offseason. His stingy at-bats -- with the patience to draw a walk, fight off tough pitches and shorten up and go the other way -- are examples of the offensive culture shift the Rockies are seeking. There is power potential. He has hit home runs in spurts this year, and a year's experience -- not just on the field, but dealing with the grind of a Major League season -- could lead to even more pop. -- Thomas Harding

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees' Paul Goldschmidt Has Gone From Disposable to Indispensable
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: For a short while there, it appeared that Paul Goldschmidt was a prime candidate to be left off the New York Yankees' postseason roster. The addition of Luis Garcia Jr. had completely clouded Goldschmidt's role, and it appeared that the impending returns of Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton would make the former NL MVP rather disposable. item.content:encoded:
For a short while there, it appeared that Paul Goldschmidt was a prime candidate to be left off the New York Yankees' postseason roster.
The addition of Luis Garcia Jr. had completely clouded Goldschmidt's role, and it appeared that the impending returns of Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton would make the former NL MVP rather disposable.
My, how things have changed.
Yes, Goldschmidt's at-bats have still been somewhat sparse since the arrival of Garcia at the MLB trade deadline, but with Judge and Stanton now both potentially out for the playoffs (or at least the Wild Card Series), Goldschmidt's value just increased exponentially.
Suddenly, Goldschmidt is now one of the Yankees' very best options against left-handed pitching, and he may get some starts in the playoffs now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf.
Goldschmidt has always mashed southpaws, owning a lifetime 1.006 OPS against them. This year, he is slashing .309/.404/.592 versus lefties, making him a must on New York's playoff squad.
It should also be noted that after a miserable month of July and after barely playing in August, Goldschmidt has gone 6-for-18 at the plate this month, so he is starting to rediscover his stroke as October draws near.
And with the Boston Red Sox — New York's likely Wild Card opponent — being loaded with left-handers, Goldschmidt will likely get significant playing time early on in the postseason.
In that scenario, Ben Rice would serve as the DH — a role that almost certainly would have gone to Stanton had he been available — and Goldschmidt will play over at first base. Garcia would then come off the bench as a pinch hitter against righties.
Goldschmidt's overall numbers this season look solid, as he is slashing .253/.316/.455 with 18 home runs and 50 RBI across 370 trips to the dish. Not bad for a 39-year-old.
However, a massive chunk of Goldschmidt's damage was done back in May and June, when he combined for 13 homers and 37 RBI and was a borderline All-Star.
Goldschmidt's production has nose dived since then, but he appears to be kicking it back into gear just in time for the playoffs.
And now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf, you can expect Goldschmidt to play a pivotal role.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — The Yankees’ chances of winning the AL East are on life support.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Of greater concern is whether their bullpen meltdown Sunday was just a bad day or represents cracks emerging in a heavily worked unit.
Brent Headrick served up a grand slam to Nolan Arenado in the fifth inning, flipping the game on its head and all but wrapping up the Yankees’ spot in the AL wild-card series next week after an 8-4 loss to the Diamondbacks at Chase Field.
By dropping the series finale, a game they once led 4-1, the Yankees (89-66) fell to six games back of the Rays with seven to play.
They will welcome the Rays to Yankee Stadium on Tuesday for a four-game showdown, needing a sweep to stay alive in the division race. One win by the Rays in The Bronx will secure them the AL East title.
The Yankees would then turn their attention to securing the top AL wild card, ending Sunday leading the Red Sox by 5 ¹/₂ games, though Aaron Judge’s questionable status for that series because of a calf strain looms over everything.
In the meantime, Sunday’s loss — on the heels of Saturday’s walk-off win by the Diamondbacks (82-74) — was another regrettable one after third-inning home runs by Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones had staked them to a 4-1 lead.
In the bottom of the fifth, Will Warren loaded the bases with one out, at which point Aaron Boone called on reliable lefty Headrick for his 79th appearance of the season — the second most in the majors.
Before Sunday, Headrick had inherited 50 runners this season and allowed only five of them to score.
But after striking out the first batter he faced, Headrick walked Corbin Carroll to force in a run, which brought Arenado to the plate.
Shop Yankees Merch
Arenado crushed Headrick’s 2-0 fastball just to the left of the left field foul pole, but then straightened it out on the very next pitch (another fastball), clobbering a grand slam to put the Diamondbacks ahead 6-4.
The Diamondbacks later added a pair of insurance runs off John Schreiber in the seventh inning, the first earned runs Schreiber has allowed as a Yankee.

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge fue retirado del enfrentamiento de los Yankees contra los Twins el miércoles durante la sexta entrada. Estaba por tomar su tercer turno al bat del juego cuando fue sustituido por Heliot Ramos. El viernes, fue colocado oficialmente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha, lo que lo mantendrá fuera hasta el final de la temporada regular y posiblemente durante parte de la postemporada.
Aunque se trata de un duro golpe para los Yankees, Judge está lejos de ser el único jugador destacado que enfrenta una lesión de cara a la postemporada. Echemos un vistazo a la situación actual en la lista de lesionados de cada equipo contendiente mientras se acerca la postemporada, destacando a algunos jugadores importantes que actualmente están fuera y ofreciendo la información más reciente sobre cuándo se espera que regresen, si es que lo hacen.
Te puede interesar: Evaluando a los Yankees sin Aaron Judge y la extraña caída de Kyle Tucker
Braves
Reynaldo Lopez, SP
Lopez tuvo problemas contra los Cubs el lunes y fue retirado del juego después de tres entradas; posteriormente fue colocado en la lista de lesionados debido a molestias en el hombro derecho, una dolencia que, según reportes, ha sufrido durante toda la temporada. Lopez se perdió prácticamente toda la temporada de 2025 debido a una lesión en el hombro y, a pesar de las molestias persistentes derivadas de ese problema, lanzó en 26 juegos este año, incluidas 13 aperturas, y registra una ERA de 4.54. El equipo no ha dado ninguna indicación sobre su estado para la postemporada, pero no parece probable que esté disponible para lanzar en octubre, lo que reduciría aún más las opciones de Atlanta en su rotación abridora.
Bryce Elder, SP
Elder fue colocado en la lista de lesionados el 9 de septiembre y se sometió a una cirugía artroscópica de rodilla, aunque se espera que solo se pierda entre tres y cuatro semanas de acción. Había estado lidiando con molestias en la rodilla desde el All-Star break y podría estar en condiciones de regresar en octubre, aunque Atlanta podría necesitar avanzar profundamente en la postemporada para que Elder alcance a regresar.
Phillies
Jesus Luzardo, SP
Luzardo fue colocado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días el martes debido a una inflamación en el hombro. Será elegible para ser activado el 27 de septiembre, el último día de la temporada regular. Está por verse si estará listo para regresar en ese momento, pero el equipo confía en contar con el pitcher zurdo All-Star en la postemporada. Después de ser colocado en la lista de lesionados, Luzardo dijo a los reporteros que el plan es que pueda lanzar en octubre.
Brad Keller, RP
Keller estará fuera hasta 2027 después de sufrir un desgarro del UCL en el codo de lanzar, dejando fuera por el resto de la temporada a uno de los relevistas importantes de los Phillies. En 32 apariciones esta temporada, Keller registró una ERA de 4.02, con 32 strikeouts, 13 bases por bolas y tres salvamentos en 31 1/3 entradas.
Brewers
Brandon Woodruff, SP
Woodruff está fuera desde el 5 de julio, pero todavía existe una pequeña posibilidad de que pueda regresar en la parte final de la temporada. Woodruff está lidiando con una lesión en la cápsula del hombro derecho, aunque tuvo un buen desempeño durante la primera mitad de la campaña. En nueve aperturas, el pitcher de 33 años registró una ERA de 2.98, con 47 strikeouts y apenas 10 bases por bolas en 45 1/3 entradas. No está claro qué papel podría asumir para Milwaukee en la postemporada después de perderse casi tres meses completos, aunque podría aportar entradas valiosas desde el bullpen si el equipo considera que todavía no está listo para asumir la carga de trabajo de un abridor.
Cubs
Justin Steele, SP
Steele no ha lanzado en MLB desde abril del año pasado, después de atravesar una larga ausencia debido a una lesión en el codo del brazo con el que lanza. Actualmente se encuentra en rehabilitación en Triple A, pero el equipo pretende que haga algunas apariciones más antes de potencialmente activarlo de cara a la postemporada, tomando en cuenta cuánto tiempo ha pasado desde que lanzó en un juego de MLB. El manager Craig Counsell dijo que el equipo está “contento con lo que está sucediendo. Pero [Steele] va a necesitar lanzar más”, antes de regresar.
Ben Brown, SP
La temporada de Brown terminó después de sufrir una lesión en el cuello y experimentar un retroceso en su recuperación tras una sesión de lanzamientos en el complejo de spring training del equipo en Arizona a finales de agosto. No podrá regresar para la postemporada y, en cambio, se concentrará en estar listo para la campaña de 2027.
Dodgers
Shohei Ohtani, SP/DH
Ohtani ha estado lidiando con lesiones en la rodilla izquierda y el bíceps derecho y fue colocado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días. No ha lanzado desde el 3 de julio debido al estrés que soporta su rodilla lesionada cuando lanza desde el montículo. Será elegible para regresar de la lista de lesionados el 23 de septiembre, y el manager Dave Roberts ha indicado que espera que Ohtani vuelva a jugar antes de que concluya la temporada regular. Ohtani dijo que se concentrará en batear cuando regrese a la acción y que probablemente no volverá a lanzar en 2026.
Dalton Rushing, C
El catcher suplente de los Dodgers tuvo mucha actividad detrás del plato durante la prolongada ausencia de Will Smith, pero fue colocado en la lista de lesionados el 6 de septiembre debido a molestias en el codo derecho, derivadas de un desgarro parcial del UCL. El equipo ha dicho que Rushing no volverá a desempeñarse como catcher esta temporada, pero mantiene la esperanza de que pueda contribuir como bateador designado o bateador emergente durante la postemporada.
Edwin Diaz, RP
Las lesiones han obstaculizado la primera temporada de Diaz con los Dodgers, y volvió a la lista de lesionados a mediados de agosto después de una mala racha de actuaciones. Se espera que el pitcher de 32 años regrese el viernes, aunque parece que el equipo todavía no ha decidido si siquiera estará en el roster de postemporada, tomando en cuenta sus problemas durante el año. Diaz registra una poco atractiva ERA de 11.85 esta temporada, con siete salvamentos y 19 strikeouts en 13 2/3 entradas. Si Diaz no logra mostrar cierto nivel de estabilidad sobre el montículo durante el tramo final, podría no estar en los planes del equipo para octubre.
Andy Pages, CF
Pages está en la lista de lesionados desde el 22 de agosto debido a una fractura en la mano izquierda, pero se espera que regrese antes del final de la temporada regular y probablemente no necesite una asignación de rehabilitación. Pages estaba teniendo el mejor año de su carrera antes de la lesión, con 21 home runs, 80 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de .797. Si regresa a la acción sin contratiempos, Pages debería estar listo para la postemporada y recuperar su puesto como center fielder titular de Los Angeles.
Roki Sasaki, SP/RP
Una ampolla en el dedo medio de la mano derecha llevó a Sasaki a la lista de lesionados a finales de agosto, pero se acerca a su regreso después de realizar el miércoles una sesión de bullpen con bateadores. Estará disponible para la postemporada, pero todavía no se ha determinado qué papel tendrá. Jack Harris, de California Post, reporta que es probable que Sasaki lance desde el bullpen en octubre, aunque podría ser utilizado en la rotación en caso de que se presente una lesión de un pitcher hacia el final de la temporada.
Blake Snell, SP
Snell abandonó su apertura del miércoles debido a un problema en la ingle, pero no está claro si necesitará pasar por la lista de lesionados como consecuencia. Snell hizo su debut de temporada el 9 de mayo, pero fue colocado en la lista de lesionados debido a una lesión en el codo. No regresó sino hasta el 11 de agosto, después de lo cual realizó seis aperturas antes de que surgiera el problema en la ingle durante su más reciente salida. No está claro si volverá al montículo durante la temporada regular, ya que los Dodgers probablemente priorizarán mantenerlo saludable para la postemporada.
Padres
Gavin Sheets, DH
Sheets está fuera de acción desde finales de agosto mientras lidia con un esguince en el pie, pero retomó el swing a mediados de septiembre y podría estar listo para regresar en la postemporada. La expectativa, de acuerdo con AJ Cassavell, de MLB.com, es que Sheets regrese como bateador designado o bateador emergente y no juegue a la defensiva en octubre.
Joe Musgrove, SP
Musgrove no ha realizado una apertura desde 2024, debido a que atraviesa una larga recuperación de una cirugía Tommy John. Mientras intentaba aumentar gradualmente su carga de trabajo durante su rehabilitación en las Ligas Menores, Musgrove ha experimentado problemas durante la recuperación de su brazo operado. Todavía es posible que regrese antes del final de la temporada, aunque en esta etapa parece más probable que tenga un papel desde el bullpen.
Rays
Shane McClanahan, SP
McClanahan fue colocado en la lista de lesionados el 4 de septiembre después de abandonar su apertura debido a rigidez en el antebrazo. McClanahan dijo en ese momento que no creía que la lesión fuera demasiado seria, pero los Rays decidieron ser cautelosos con su pitcher estrella. La expectativa es que McClanahan esté listo para volver a lanzar antes del final de la temporada, por lo que debería estar disponible en octubre si no sufre un retroceso.
Tyler Wells, RP
Wells también fue colocado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días debido a rigidez en el antebrazo izquierdo el 15 de septiembre, y se espera que necesite permanecer el tiempo mínimo fuera antes de regresar para la postemporada. Ha sido una pieza importante del bullpen de los Rays desde que llegó en un intercambio con los Orioles, por lo que contar nuevamente con él en octubre será importante para Tampa.
Yankees
Aaron Judge, RF
Judge fue retirado del juego del miércoles contra los Twins debido a lo que el equipo describió como rigidez en la parte baja de la pierna. Se pudo ver al bateador haciendo una mueca de dolor después de un swing sin contacto durante el juego y fue retirado antes de su tercer turno al bat. El viernes, los Yankees lo colocaron oficialmente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Esto lo mantendrá fuera hasta el final de la temporada regular y posiblemente durante parte de la postemporada. Judge se perdió 84 juegos esta temporada mientras lidiaba con una lesión en las costillas, pero esta es una dolencia completamente diferente. Los aficionados en Nueva York estarán conteniendo la respiración mientras esperan una actualización más detallada sobre el estado del tres veces MVP, pero se trata de una gran preocupación para el equipo con la postemporada a poco más de una semana de distancia.
Giancarlo Stanton, DH
Stanton continúa fuera después de lesionarse la pantorrilla a principios de esta temporada y posteriormente sufrir una dolencia en la otra pantorrilla mientras se recuperaba. Stanton todavía no ha sido descartado para el resto de la temporada, aunque el equipo no ha proporcionado mucha información sobre su estado. El slugger, propenso a las lesiones, solo ha disputado 24 juegos esta temporada y no juega desde finales de abril, por lo que su disponibilidad para la postemporada continúa en duda.
Trent Grisham, CF
Grisham sufrió una distensión de Grado 2 en el tendón de la corva derecho y está en la lista de lesionados desde el 5 de septiembre. El equipo no espera que el outfielder regrese antes del final de la temporada regular, pero todavía no se ha definido su disponibilidad para la postemporada. Grisham disputó 121 juegos este año y registró 18 home runs y 59 carreras impulsadas, con un OPS de .703.
Fernando Cruz, RP
El relevista de los Yankees fue diagnosticado con un desgarro parcial del UCL en el codo derecho. Aunque no se ha recomendado una cirugía, Cruz todavía no ha reanudado sus lanzamientos, por lo que su disponibilidad para la postemporada está en duda. El veterano registra una ERA de 3.13, con 67 strikeouts en 54 2/3 entradas esta temporada, además de dos salvamentos.
Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B
Chisholm está en la lista de lesionados desde el 10 de septiembre después de sufrir un esguince en el pulgar, pero se espera que regrese a la acción antes del final de la temporada regular. Chisholm dijo a los reporteros que tiene como objetivo regresar el 22 de septiembre, antes de que los Yankees comiencen una serie final como locales contra los Rays y Orioles. Esta temporada, Chisholm ha estado aproximadamente en el promedio de la liga a la ofensiva, mientras registra un porcentaje de slugging de .403, el más bajo de su carrera, con 19 home runs, pero ha robado 40 bases, igualando la cifra más alta de su carrera.
Red Sox
Garrett Crochet, SP
Crochet ha estado fuera durante la mayor parte del año debido a una lesión en el hombro izquierdo, pero el equipo todavía tiene la esperanza de que pueda regresar para la postemporada. Crochet realizó el martes una sesión de bullpen de 30 lanzamientos y existe la posibilidad de que haga una aparición durante la temporada regular para prepararse para los playoffs. Cuando regrese con Boston, sin embargo, se espera que sea utilizado desde el bullpen, ya que no tendrá suficiente tiempo para aumentar gradualmente su carga de trabajo como abridor.
Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela sufrió una distensión en el cuádriceps durante la primera semana de septiembre, pero parece estar cerca de regresar a la acción antes del final de la temporada regular. Rafaela bateó el jueves contra una máquina Trajekt y podría participar en un juego de rehabilitación con Triple A Worcester durante el fin de semana antes de reincorporarse a los Red Sox durante la última serie como locales del equipo.
Tanner Houck, RP
Houck no ha lanzado desde mayo de 2025, pero se acerca a su regreso después de la larga recuperación que implica una cirugía Tommy John. Realizó una aparición de rehabilitación con Triple A Worcester el martes y cada vez está más cerca de regresar a las Mayores. Cuando vuelva a los Red Sox, al igual que Crochet, se espera que lance desde el bullpen durante la postemporada.
Guardians
Rhys Hoskins, 1B/DH
Hoskins fue colocado en la lista de lesionados de 10 días el 19 de agosto debido a una inflamación en la parte baja de la espalda, pero desde entonces recibió autorización para comenzar una progresión de bateo mientras avanza en su recuperación. El equipo espera que Hoskins esté listo para octubre, aunque no está claro si será activado de la lista de lesionados antes del final de la temporada regular.
Astros
Carlos Correa, IF
Correa no regresará esta temporada después de decidir esta semana que se concentrará en recuperarse para 2027. El shortstop está fuera desde mayo, cuando se sometió a una cirugía en el tobillo izquierdo. Existía cierta esperanza de que pudiera regresar a finales de esta temporada, pero parece que no asumirá el riesgo y, en cambio, se concentrará en el próximo año.
Rangers
Joc Pederson, DH
Pederson recibió un pelotazo en la mano durante el enfrentamiento del 12 de septiembre contra los Diamondbacks, aunque está intentando jugar pese a la lesión con los Rangers en plena pelea por el título de la AL West. Recibirá tratamiento mientras busca combatir la inflamación en la mano y probablemente solo estará en el lineup contra pitchers derechos.
Publicado originalmente en www.sportsillustrated.com el 18/09/2026, traducido al español para SI México.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Brian Cashman foolishly built a Yankees roster that couldn't support Aaron Judge's return
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: From June 1 through the August 3 deadline, the New York Yankees were hurting for offense. The club ranked 28th during that span in OPS with a .672 mark. As a result, Brian Cashman went out and bolstered the offense. He acquired Heliot Ramos, who was brutal at the start of his tenure in New York, but has bounced back over the past three weeks. R
item.content:encoded:
From June 1 through the August 3 deadline, the New York Yankees were hurting for offense. The club ranked 28th during that span in OPS with a .672 mark. They were 26th in runs scored with 214, an average of 3.96 per game during that 54-game period. The Yankees collectively slashed a putrid .221/.283/.389.
As a result, Brian Cashman went out and bolstered the offense. He acquired Heliot Ramos, who was brutal at the start of his tenure in New York, but has bounced back over the past three weeks. Ramos, though, was an upgrade on the margins as a platoon bat brought into mash lefties. The real get was former Washington Nationals first baseman Luis Garcia Jr.
Garcia Jr. has looked like a budding star, so this next part is tough. He joined an already crowded first base-DH rotation that includes a fringe MVP candidate in Ben Rice and a former MVP who still plays like one against lefties, Paul Goldschmidt, with a 1.006 OPS this season against southpaws.
It made sense, except for one gigantic looming development. The Yankees were expecting to get Aaron Judge back before the end of the season, who would have a much greater impact on New York's offensive output than any external addition could have by a wide margin.
That created a situation that when Judge returned after missing over three months of action, he'd immediately have to jump back in to right field. The Yankees were unable to protect his body and easy him back in at DH thanks to the logjam Cashman created, and as a result, Judge is heading back to the IL after just seven games back. Now, his status for the playoffs is in peril.
Brian Cashman's lack of trade deadline vision put Aaron Judge and the Yankees' World Series hopes at risk
First, a caveat. Judge could have wound up with a calf injury even if he wasn't playing right field. We can get into whether or not he needed more time to ramp up and was brought back too fast, but that's a discussion for another day.
The fact of the matter is that Cashman went out at the deadline and reconstructed the roster in such a way that Judge could only play right field upon his return. That was a mistake.
Now, the market wasn't exactly flush with options, but with some creativity and a willingness to be bold, Cashman could have still completed the necessary task of upgrading the offense while ensuring Judge could be protected by being inserted into the DH spot upon activation.
For example, rather than relying on George Lombard Jr. to man shortstop and provide a spark, he could have gone out and gotten an established young star at the position like Zach Neto or CJ Abrams. Neither player moved at the deadline, but for the right package, they would have. It might have cost Lombard Jr. to get it done, but as we've seen sometimes holding on to even the best prospects can end poorly.
Another lever Cashman could've pulled would've been flexing the franchise's financial might and absorbing Rafael Devers' contract. Yes, Devers just underwent season-ending core muscle surgery, but his blistering .275/.375/.611 second-half performance would have at least bridged the gap until Judge was ready, and perhaps he wouldn't have suffered the same fate had he been dealt here.
Devers has played mostly first base and DH, but while he's not a great third baseman, that's where he has the most experience, and he could've benefited from playing next to the rangy Lombard Jr. Maybe not an ideal solution, but it would've solved the logjam.
Lastly, he could have thought outside the box and beat the Dodgers offer for Tarik Skubal. This wouldn't have helped the offense, but hey, if you struggle to score, you can still win if you make it even harder for your opponent to scratch runs across. In the meantime, the coaching staff could try to figure out why the bats had been so putrid yet hit the third-most homers in MLB (76) during that otherwise horrendous 54-game stretch.
At the end of the day, Cashman did what he always does and went out and got the controllable player with projection over the established star in order to keep his prospect cost down. As a result, he created a logjam that put unnecessary risk on his three-time MVP. If Judge isn't ready in time for the start of October baseball, it will be a devastating blow to the Yankees' World Series aspirations, and it was all completely avoidable.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Why Cam Schlittler was pissed at himself after NY's loss to Diamondbacks appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Cam Schlittler wasn't happy with his performance on the mound after the New York Yankees' 5-3 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday night.
Schlittler is going through the second season of his career in the majors with the Yankees. He has quickly broken out as one of the best young pitchers, helping New York be firm in the playoff picture this year.
Schlittler started on the mound as he lasted six innings, striking out six batters while conceding three hits and one earned run. New York lost on Pavin Smith's pinch-hit, two-run homer in the ninth inning, resulting in Arizona's victory. He blamed himself for those mistakes after the game.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"I mean, I wouldn't say I really gave them a chance,'' Schlittler said. "That one's kind of on me, so I'll take the blame for that. Made an error there, let up two runs."
"I mean, there's still a chance,'' Schlittler said, "but we got to play our (butts) off a little bit.'
How Cam Schlittler, Yankees played against Diamondbacks
Cam Schlittler and the Yankees have preparation for the postseason. These last games of the regular season will decide their place in the AL bracket, needing every win they can get.
The game was scoreless throughout the first four innings, seeing both teams finally get on the board in the fifth frame. However, Arizona dealt more blows as New York was unable to muster up more big plays to rally back against the hosts.
New York fell to an 89-65 record on the season, sitting at second place in the AL East Division standings. They are above the Boston Red Sox and the Toronto Blue Jays while trailing the Tampa Bay Rays.
The Yankees will look to bounce back in their series finale against the Diamondbacks. That contest commences on Sept. 20 at 4:10 p.m. ET.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Yankees' Aaron Judge injury updates from Judge, Aaron Boone feel purposely vague
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: Eagle-eyed New York Yankees beat writers stalked the field for any signs of Aaron Judge's post-injury workouts on Sunday, in the same way that both Cody Bellinger and Trent Grisham were back on the grass testing their agility shortly after coming up lame. No such luck with Judge; the Yankees kept him in the shadows instead. That shouldn't be surprising. Judge kept his timeline under lock and key throughout his entire rib injury rehab process (though somehow the Rockies series managed to emerge a
item.content:encoded:
Eagle-eyed New York Yankees beat writers stalked the field for any signs of Aaron Judge's post-injury workouts on Sunday, in the same way that both Cody Bellinger and Trent Grisham were back on the grass testing their agility shortly after coming up lame. No such luck with Judge; the Yankees kept him in the shadows instead. That shouldn't be surprising.
Judge kept his timeline under lock and key throughout his entire rib injury rehab process (though somehow the Rockies series managed to emerge as an accurate target along the way). His reinjury just one week after returning to the lineup has thrown both his rehab plan and playoff availability into question, with detectives looking to ding him retroactively for his process and dig into the future simultaneously.
It's no wonder that information about Judge's new injury has come in drips and drabs. The only thing Judge has been willing to give the media so far is the information that it's the soleus muscle that he hurt, which makes baseball motions difficult and could lead to a more progressive and harrowing injury down the line under the wrong circumstances.
But what grade is it? Is a 2-3 week timeline typical, or is it something much worse? Judge won't say, only betraying that he'd like to be back for the postseason.
Get it? If he never admits the grade, he doesn't remove himself from consideration for the Wild Card series outright. Very clever. Not reassuring.
Aaron Boone doesn't help Yankees fans learn more about Aaron Judge calf strain
If you were hoping to ply the information Judge has refused to give out of Aaron Boone, you weren't any luckier by choosing that path. Instead of cheeky optimism, though, you would've received frustrated bluster.
If Judge says he wants to be back for October, then Boone will neither refute nor endorse that notion. Instead, he'll give you the curt half-truth.
He'll be back. Or he won't. The only two options.
The Yankees and Judge will never say it, both to betray their competitive advantage and their beloved captain, but a return in the Wild Card series feels somewhere between foolish and impossible. A return during the postseason will depend on many factors, most of them related to how far this team is able to push without Judge's star power and added gravity. If you're looking for clarity here, maybe you can find it in between the Yankees' public statements.

item.title: [Excélsior] Yankees sueñan con Aaron Judge en playoffs
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Campa
item.description: Los Yankees de Nueva York mantienen viva la esperanza de recuperar a Aaron Judge para los playoffs, aunque el regreso de su capitán dependerá de cómo evolucione durante los últimos días de la temporada regular. Judge fue colocado nuevamente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días después de que una resonancia magnética reveló una distensión en el músculo sóleo, ubicado en la parte baja de la pantorrilla. La lesión afecta principalmente su capacidad para correr y, por ahora, el poderoso bateador no
item.content:encoded:
Los Yankees de Nueva York mantienen viva la esperanza de recuperar a Aaron Judge para los playoffs, aunque el regreso de su capitán dependerá de cómo evolucione durante los últimos días de la temporada regular. 
Judge fue colocado nuevamente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días después de que una resonancia magnética reveló una distensión en el músculo sóleo, ubicado en la parte baja de la pantorrilla. La lesión afecta principalmente su capacidad para correr y, por ahora, el poderoso bateador no tiene una fecha definida para volver a la alineación. 
“Me gustaría estar de vuelta para la postemporada”, reconoció Judge, seleccionado ocho veces al Juego de Estrellas, quien aseguró que continuará realizando todos los entrenamientos posibles con la intención de estar disponible en octubre.
El escenario todavía permite cierto optimismo para los Yankees. Judge podrá ser reactivado para el último partido de la temporada regular, programado para el 27 de septiembre, aunque eso no significa que necesariamente estará listo para jugar ese día. 
La nueva lesión llegó apenas una semana después de que Judge regresó de una fractura de costilla que lo mantuvo fuera de actividad durante más de tres meses. Desde su vuelta acumuló cuatro hits en 23 turnos, con 13 ponches y un extrabase en siete partidos. En toda la temporada únicamente ha participado en 66 encuentros. 
La ausencia del capitán ha acompañado a Nueva York durante buena parte de la campaña. Los Yankees presentan marca de 41-25 en los partidos en los que Judge estuvo disponible, mientras que tienen récord de 48-39 cuando el toletero no formó parte de la alineación. 
Aaron Boone, mánager de los Yankees, evitó ponerle una fecha al regreso de su estrella y señaló que la decisión dependerá exclusivamente de la respuesta de su cuerpo durante la recuperación.
Judge, por su parte, admitió la frustración que representa volver a quedar fuera después de una ausencia tan prolongada, especialmente porque su intención era disputar algunos encuentros antes del inicio de la postemporada.
Para los Yankees, el tiempo comienza a convertirse en el principal rival. La temporada regular entra en sus últimos días y el objetivo ahora es conseguir que Judge pueda estar disponible cuando llegue octubre, incluso si eso significa hacerlo sin demasiados partidos de preparación.
Nueva York ya piensa en los playoffs. Y una parte importante de sus aspiraciones pasa por volver a colocar a Aaron Judge en el corazón de su alineación.

item.title: [cubbiescrib.com] Cubs magic number ticks lower, but home-field advantage is far from locked up
item.dc:creator: Jake Misener

item.content:encoded:
On a night dedicated to the 2001 World Series champions, the Arizona Diamondbacks fittingly walked off the Aaron Judge-less New York Yankees. That win, paired with a Chicago Cubs victory over the Cincinnati Reds, has the Cubs' magic number to clinch a playoff spot at just 2 with a week to go in the regular season.
That means any combination of two Cubs' wins and Diamondbacks' losses punches the former's playoff ticket, sending Chicago back to the postseason for the second consecutive season. It would take a catastrophic turn of events for that to not happen at this point. But the Cubs have their sights set on a higher prize: the #4 seed and home-field advantage in the Wild Card Series.
Home-field advantage is critical for the three teams ahead of Arizona in the wild-card standings. The Cubs and Padres enter Sunday tied for the first spot at 86-69 and the Phillies are hot on their heels at 85-70. Wodering why getting that top spot is so important? Just look at each team's home record:
- Cubs: 45-33
- Padres: 48-29
- Phillies: 41-34
Home-field advantage is critical to Cubs' World Series aspirations
Last postseason, the Cubs went 4-1 at Wrigley Field, taking down the Padres in the Wild Card Series and winning both of the games against Milwaukee in Chicago, as well. What they don't want to do is have to go to Philly or San Diego as the road team. The Padres are cooking at Petco Park of late, winning 22 of 27.
The Cubs go for a series win over the Reds on Sunday afternoon, then have a scheduled off-day Monday before returning home for the final home series of the regular season - a three-game set against Miami. Chicago then heads to Boston to close out the year against the Red Sox.
Looking at the rest of the NL playoff picture, the Brewers already locked up a fourth consecutive NL Central title and the Dodgers have won the NL West. Atlanta is knocking on the door of a division crown in the National League East, so it'll be all eyes on the wild-card race as the 2026 regular season draws to a close.

item.dc:creator: Cole Shelton

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees avoided a major injury to star outfielder Spencer Jones.
Jones didn't play on Saturday due to an injury; it isn't considered long-term
New York is coming off a 5-3 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday, as the Yankees will look for the series win on Sunday.
New York Yankees Get Injury Update on Spencer Jones
After Jones didn't play on Saturday due to an injury, there was some concern about him. New York is already without Aaron Judge, so losing Jones before the playoffs begin would be a blow.
Yet, the injury to Jones doesn't seem serious, according to the MLB.com injury report, as he was available off the bench.
"Jammed his heel during Twins series earlier in the week, Jones said Sept. 19. Could be available off the bench," the injury report read.
The hope for the Yankees is Jones could return to the lineup on Sunday, or Tuesday when they begin a series against the Tampa Bay Rays. They could opt to give Jones another day off on Sunday to give him three full days off to make sure his jammed heel is fully healthy.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone, meanwhile, confirmed Jones was available off the bench on Saturday if needed.
"He was available, like I would've… if a spot came up to hit or we needed to do something I would've gone to him," Boone said.
Jones also said the injury was no big deal and doesn't need an IL stint.
Jones is hitting .248 with 10 home runs and 38 RBIs with the Yankees this season in 80 games in his first MLB season.
New York Right Now
The Yankees will be a Wild Card team again this year but could be without star slugger Aaron Judge.
Judge is back on the IL due to a right calf strain and he said he hopes he can return for the playoffs.
"I'd like to be back by the postseason," Judge said. "That's definitely the plan. [It's the] 10-day IL, so the 10th day is probably the last game of the season. So we'll see. I've got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that."
Judge doesn't know the grade of the strain, but is confident he can return for the playoffs.
"I've dealt with strains before and kind of played through them, but this was kind of in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult," Judge said.
The Yankees are 89-65 and 5 games back of the Rays for the top spot in the AL East.
This article was originally published on HEAVY

item.content:encoded:
After watching star slugger Aaron Judge return to the plate, fans hoped he'd help the New York Yankees as they wrap up their regular season.
But now, he's back on the IL, and new details have emerged.
Yankees Provide Latest Aaron Judge Update
According to MLB analyst Jim Bowden of The Athletic, the 34-year-old outfielder has been diagnosed with a "soleus strain which is a strain of the deeper calf muscle underneath the gastrocnemius."
He added, "Typical recovery is 2-6 weeks. Soleus strains often times linger because it's the muscle that works every time you stand/walk etc. Yanks have not shared the grade."
Aaron Judge calf injury is a soleus strain which is a strain of the deeper calf muscle underneath the gastrocnemius. Typical recovery is 2-6 weeks. Soleus strains often times linger because it's the muscle that works every time you stand/walk etc. Yanks have not shared the grade.
— Jim Bowden⚾️ (@JimBowdenGM) September 20, 2026
Since returning to the plate on Sept. 8, he's appeared in seven games.
He played in two against the Colorado Rockies, three against the New York Mets and two against the Minnesota Twins.
His last appearance was on Sept. 16.

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge’s second-half stretch lasted all of seven games, and now the New York Yankees are facing the very real possibility of being without their superstar slugger for the remainder of their season, regardless of how much longer it lasts.
The Bronx Bombers’ captain has suffered a calf strain, landing him on the 10-day injured list and ending his regular season. Whether or not he can make it back at any point this postseason remains to be seen, but that is the goal for the 34-year-old.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Judge said, adding that he does not know the grade of the strain. “That’s definitely the plan. [It’s the] 10-day IL, so the 10th day is probably the last game of the season. So we’ll see. I’ve got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that.”
It’s wishful thinking, especially considering calf strains held out two of New York’s other big baseball stars across for an extended stretch earlier this season. Ex-Yankee Juan Soto missed over a month with a low-grade calf strain, while shortstop Francisco Lindor missed two months.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone did not offer much more insight when asked about Judge’s future.
“It doesn’t matter what grade it is. We have nine games left,” Boone said. “We’re going to get him back, or we’re not. That’s what we’re going to work to do, and we’ll see.”
As things stand, the Yankees’ postseason begins in the American League Wild Card Series on Sept. 29, where they will host the Boston Red Sox in the three-game series for a second consecutive year.

item.content:encoded:
One thing is to begin the 2026 MLB playoffs at full strength; another is to enter them shorthanded. The New York Yankees recently suffered another injury setback involving Aaron Judge. While the No.99 could not provide an exact timeline for his return, he made it clear that his goal is to be back for the postseason.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason. That’s definitely the plan,” Judge said per MLB insider Bryan Hoch on X. “I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that.”
With only a few days remaining in the regular season, Aaron Boone is analyzing every step to take from here on out. Will he ultimately be able to count on one of his biggest stars when the most decisive stage of the season begins for the Pinstripes?
Another setback for Aaron Judge
Aaron Judge landed back on the 10-day injured list after suffering a right calf strain during Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins. He felt tightness in his lower right leg in the first inning and was ultimately pulled in the sixth, with an MRI on Thursday revealing the strain in his soleus muscle.
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees looks on.
It’s a brutal blow for the Yanks given that Judge had literally just returned a week prior from a three-month absence due to a fractured rib, putting his availability for the rest of the regular season and the upcoming postseason run in serious doubt.
What comes next for the Yankees without Judge?
With the regular season winding down, the New York Yankees wrap up their final stretch back at the Bronx, hosting a crucial four-game set against the Tampa Bay Rays before finishing out the schedule with a three-game home series against the Baltimore Orioles. Sitting comfortably at the top of the Wild Card standings, New York is pretty much locked in for October baseball and looking as the prime favorite to hold down the #4 seed.
That setup means they would host the entire best-of-three Wild Card Series right at Yankee Stadium, where they’re currently on track to lock horns with either their archrival Boston Red Sox or whichever contender grabs that last spot—likely a hard-nosed AL Central club like the Cleveland Guardians or Chicago White Sox.

item.description: D-backs strive to make more 'magic' happen vs. Yankees (Photo credit: Matt Kartozian) Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said he felt 'a little bit of magic' in a 5-3 walk-off win over the New York Yankees on Saturday, the night the Diamondbacks celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series title. item.content:encoded:
D-backs strive to make more 'magic' happen vs. Yankees
(Photo credit: Matt Kartozian)
Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said he felt 'a little bit of magic' in a 5-3 walk-off win over the New York Yankees on Saturday, the night the Diamondbacks celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series title.
The Diamondbacks will take wins however they can get them as they continue an uphill fight for a National League wild-card berth in Sunday afternoon's finale of a three-game series vs. the Yankees in Phoenix.
New York's Will Warren (10-6, 3.89 ERA) will oppose Arizona's Corbin Burnes (0-0, 5.87) in a battle of right-handers.
'There was a ton of energy in the stadium,' said Lovullo, noting that most of the players from the 2001 team were on hand, 'so maybe there was a little bit of magic somewhere in these rafters that everybody picked up on.'
Pavin Smith's two-run, game-winning homer saved the Diamondbacks for a night, but work remains.
'We have to get inside a certain number,' said Lovullo, whose team will finish the regular season next week with a pair of three-game series at Colorado and San Diego. 'We know it, and this team is driving for something they feel they are able to do.'
Arizona (81-74) is five games behind the Chicago Cubs (86-69) and San Diego (86-69) and four behind Philadelphia (85-70) for the NL's three wild-card spots. Each team has seven games remaining.
The Yankees (89-65) fell five games behind first-place Tampa Bay (94-60) in the AL East. Those teams will meet in a four-game series in Yankee Stadium beginning with a split doubleheader on Tuesday and already have clinched a postseason berth.
'I have a ton of confidence in the guys we have rolling out there right now,' New York manager Aaron Boone said after Aaron Judge (calf strain) landed on the 10-day injured list Saturday.
Warren worked the Yankees' playoff clincher Monday at Minnesota, although he did not get a decision after giving up two runs (both unearned) in 5 2/3 innings of an 8-3 win. He struck out six and walked two.
Warren has been a workhorse on a staff that has faced injury issues. He will make his 29th start, second on the team behind Cam Schlittler (32).
'We've got a veteran core that's been here before, and we're looking to do big things,' Warren said of the upcoming postseason.
Warren has faced the Diamondbacks once in his career, giving up two runs on one hit -- a Corbin Carroll two-run homer -- in five innings of a no-decision on April 1, 2025.
Burnes will make his third start since being activated from the injured list Sept. 8 after a 15-month absence following Tommy John surgery. He gave up five runs in 4 2/3 innings but didn't figure into the decision in Monday's 8-7 victory over Miami, striking out four with no walks.
'It's all about cutter command,' Burnes said of his pet pitch, which he traditionally throws about 50% of the time. 'Just have to be more consistent with that,'
Burnes is 0-2 with a 1.93 ERA in four career starts against the Yankees. Paul Goldschmidt is 10-for-34 with a homer against the four-time All-Star and 2021 NL Cy Young Award winner.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Aaron Judge Admite Que La Temporada Regular Se Ha Acabado, En Medio De Un Creciente Escrutinio Por Una Decisión Errónea De Los Yankees

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees incluyeron oficialmente a Aaron Judge en la lista de lesionados de 10 días este sábado, con efecto retroactivo desde el jueves, y han llamado a Max Schuemann. Judge no podrá volver antes del 27 de septiembre, el último día de la temporada regular, y se perderá la serie de cuatro partidos contra los Rays en el Yankee Stadium.
Eso no deja casi margen para una preparación normal antes de que empiece la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana el 29 de septiembre. Judge había vuelto el 8 de septiembre tras una ausencia de 99 días por una fractura por estrés en la primera costilla derecha. Antes de la lesión en la pantorrilla, había bateado 4 de 23, con un jonrón y 13 strikeouts.
El momento es especialmente malo porque Judge acababa de empezar a recuperar su swing. El jonrón de tres carreras que bateó el lunes en Minnesota fue el primero desde que volvió. Dos días después, notó una tensión en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha durante la primera entrada, siguió en el partido y no se retiró hasta que Heliot Ramos entró como bateador suplente por él en la sexta.
Una resonancia magnética realizada en Phoenix reveló la distensión. Judge dijo el sábado que se trata del sóleo, lo que describió como «algo más grave a la hora de correr y batear». No quiso dar detalles sobre la gravedad de la lesión, y Aaron Boone volvió a negarse a dar un plazo de recuperación.
Los Yankees ya saben lo que puede suponer su ausencia. Desde el 2 de junio hasta el 7 de septiembre, Nueva York ocupó el puesto 29 de las Grandes Ligas con un wRC+ de 90 y un promedio de bateo de 0,227, el 28 en wOBA y el 27 en OPS. El pitcheo fue lo que, en gran medida, mantuvo a flote a los Yankees.
La historia reciente de los Yankees hace que sea más difícil pasar por alto esta apuesta
Los partidos de rehabilitación no garantizan la buena forma física. Su valor radica en la repetición controlada, las pruebas de recuperación y la exposición al ritmo de juego antes de que llegue la intensidad de la postemporada.
La historia reciente de los Yankees nos invita a la cautela. Matt Carpenter volvió tras una fractura en el pie para la postemporada de 2022 y acabó con un 1 de 12 y nueve strikeouts. En 2019, Edwin Encarnación volvió tras una distensión en los oblicuos y bateó .056 en la ALCS, mientras que Gary Sánchez bateó .129 tras una lesión en la ingle en septiembre.
Esos ejemplos no predicen cómo le irá a Judge, pero sí muestran por qué es importante el momento. Si está listo el 27 de septiembre, los Yankees tendrían un partido de la temporada regular antes de los playoffs. Si no, su primer partido tras la baja podría ser bajo la presión de los playoffs y sin apenas preparación en condiciones reales.
Las decisiones del juez sobre quiénes volverán están ahora en el punto de mira
La segunda lesión hizo que el debate pasara de centrarse en la mala suerte a centrarse en las decisiones relacionadas con el regreso de Judge. Él dejó claro en agosto que quería saltarse la etapa de rehabilitación en las ligas menores, y los Yankees se lo permitieron.
El juez solo se había enfrentado a lanzamientos en directo una vez antes de su reincorporación. Cuando los Yankees le limitaron a seis entradas en su regreso el 8 de septiembre, dejó claro que no le gustaba nada esa restricción, aunque el plan se había discutido de antemano.
«Respeto a Booney, así que haré lo que él diga. Pero no me hace ninguna gracia», dijo Judge después de ese partido.
Ahora esa secuencia parece un poco rara. No demuestra que una asignación de rehabilitación hubiera evitado la lesión, y Boone rechaza esa conclusión. Pero saltarse los partidos de las ligas menores y luego negarse a seguir una carga de trabajo controlada ha avivado las dudas sobre la preparación.
El juez se mantiene firme a medida que se va acabando octubre
El propio Judge les dio a los Yankees una idea más clara de su lesión el sábado, pero no el plazo que necesitan.
El capitán dijo que la distensión en la pantorrilla derecha afecta al músculo sóleo y que volver para la postemporada es «sin duda el plan». Unas horas más tarde, Nueva York perdió 5-3 contra Arizona, quedando con un balance de 89-65 y a cinco partidos de Tampa Bay, cuando quedan ocho partidos por disputar.
«Me gustaría volver para la fase final. Ese es, sin duda, el plan. La verdad es que no te puedo dar ninguna respuesta sobre plazos ni nada por el estilo», dijo Judge tras el partido.
Eso prácticamente lo dejó fuera de esta temporada regular.
Judge sigue sin cuestionar esa decisión. Ha argumentado que una asignación a rehabilitación no habría eliminado el riesgo de lesión, y el sábado volvió a defenderla después de que se hiciera oficial su paso a la lista de lesionados.
«La gente se lesiona las pantorrillas y los cuádriceps en los partidos de rehabilitación, así que no creo que saltarse un partido en la Doble A vaya a cambiar nada de eso», dijo Judge a principios de semana.
Ahora los Yankees necesitan que Judge acepte un ritmo más lento
Judge ha construido su carrera jugando a pesar de las molestias. Se cree que la lesión en las costillas se produjo el 26 de abril en una atrapada en picado en Houston, pero siguió jugando hasta el 31 de mayo. Esa competitividad forma parte de su valor, pero ahora los Yankees tienen menos posibilidades de adaptarse a ella.
Judge se ha marcado públicamente el mes de octubre como objetivo. «Me gustaría volver para la fase final. Ese es, sin duda, el plan», dijo el sábado. Pero querer algo no es lo mismo que estar preparado. Su pantorrilla aún tiene que aguantar el esfuerzo de correr, batear y jugar partidos.
Por ahora, los Yankees siguen sin tener una respuesta. Judge se perderá la serie contra los Rays, la diferencia en la clasificación de la división es de cinco partidos y Boone no ha dicho si su capitán estará listo para cuando empiece la postemporada. La próxima decisión puede ser más importante que la anterior: hasta qué punto los Yankees dejarán que Judge se exija al máximo una vez que se recupere el sóleo.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.title: [bolavip.com] Aaron Boone challenges Aaron Judge-less NY Yankees ahead of Rays series
