item.content:encoded:
El pelotero fue colocado nuevamente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha
Los New York Yankees volverán a prescindir de Aaron Judge durante la recta final de la temporada regular. El equipo anunció que el jardinero será colocado en la lista de lesionados de 10 días debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha.
La baja llega pocos días después de su regreso a las Grandes Ligas tras permanecer fuera por una fractura en una costilla. Judge había vuelto a la alineación el 8 de septiembre ante los Colorado Rockies, pero ahora deberá detener nuevamente su actividad mientras los Yankees evalúan su recuperación.
El movimiento será realizado el sábado y podrá hacerse retroactivo al jueves, por lo que, bajo ese escenario, el jugador podría estar disponible para el último partido de la temporada regular, programado para el 27 de septiembre.
Aaron Judge vuelve a sufrir una lesión tras su regreso
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Brewers conquistan por cuarto año consecutivo la División Central de la Liga Nacional
Judge abandonó el encuentro del miércoles ante los Minnesota Twins después de presentar rigidez en la parte baja de la pierna derecha. Una entrada antes había tenido que desplazarse hacia los jardines para intentar capturar una pelota, aunque no mostró dificultades durante la jugada.
El propio jugador explicó después del encuentro que había sentido las primeras molestias desde la primera entrada y que decidió continuar para intentar permanecer en el partido.
“Intenté seguir y ver cuánto tiempo podíamos aguantar, porque estos partidos son importantes en esta parte de la temporada. Pero después de hablarlo, pensé que lo correcto era salir para no perjudicar al equipo en el campo o en las bases”, explicó.
La lesión representa otro periodo de inactividad para Judge, quien pasó más de tres meses fuera debido a una fractura en la costilla derecha que, de acuerdo con los reportes, sufrió el 26 de abril durante un partido en Houston.
El jugador continuó participando con la lesión durante aproximadamente un mes antes de ingresar a la lista de lesionados después del encuentro del 31 de mayo frente a los Athletics.
El regreso de Judge duró seis partidos
Judge volvió a la actividad sin pasar por una asignación de rehabilitación en las Ligas Menores. Su regreso ocurrió el 8 de septiembre ante Colorado, pero tuvo dificultades para recuperar su producción ofensiva durante los encuentros posteriores.
En sus primeros seis partidos después de regresar registró cuatro imparables en 23 turnos, con un cuadrangular. Posteriormente disputó un séptimo encuentro antes de sufrir la molestia en la pantorrilla. Desde su vuelta, terminó con 4 hits en 26 turnos, 13 ponches y un extrabase.
Antes de su nueva lesión, Judge había participado en 66 partidos durante la temporada y registraba un promedio de bateo de .241, con 18 cuadrangulares y 41 carreras producidas.
Yankees afrontan el cierre sin Judge
La baja de Judge llega cuando Nueva York ya aseguró al menos un lugar en el Comodín de la Liga Americana, aunque todavía mantiene actividad en la pelea por el liderato de la División Este. Los Yankees se encuentran cinco juegos por detrás de los Tampa Bay Rays, líderes de la división, al comenzar la jornada del viernes.
Judge, actual Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana y tres veces ganador del premio, tendrá ahora que enfocarse en su recuperación. Los Yankees, mientras tanto, deberán afrontar los últimos encuentros de la temporada regular sin una de sus principales piezas ofensivas y con la posibilidad de que su regreso ocurra hasta los últimos días del calendario.

item.title: [New York Post] Aaron Judge lands on IL with calf strain in Yankees nightmare — as huge playoff question emerges
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description: Aaron Judge is going on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain, the Yankees announced Friday, just seven games after he returned from a three-month stay on the IL with a right rib stress fracture. Access the Yankees beat like never before Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees. With only nine games left in the regular season after Friday, Judge’s injury threatens to be a serious blow to t
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge is going on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain, the Yankees announced Friday, just seven games after he returned from a three-month stay on the IL with a right rib stress fracture.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
With only nine games left in the regular season after Friday, Judge’s injury threatens to be a serious blow to the Yankees’ October hopes and dreams.
The earliest Judge can be activated off the IL — he will officially be placed on it Saturday, but retroactive to Thursday — is in time for Game 162, though there is doubt over whether he will even be ready in time for the start of the playoffs.
“I don’t know,” Aaron Boone said Friday at Chase Field.
Boone would not divulge a timeline for Judge, nor the grade of his strain. But after he received treatment on his calf during Thursday’s off day, it became clear there was not enough improvement, at which point they decided to send him for tests that revealed the strain.
The AL wild-card series, which the Yankees are all but assured to play in with their chances of catching the Rays for the division slim, begins on Sept. 29. Once again, Judge will be racing the clock to try to get back in time, creating major concerns for the Yankees as they head down the stretch without their best player.
“There’s no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations that don’t change now,” Boone said. “We have a lot of confidence in the people we run out there every day and how we’re going to match up day in and day out, and the goal doesn’t change.”
When Judge spent most of the summer months on the IL, the Yankees’ offense largely cratered without him, though they had started to break out of their malaise shortly before he returned on Sept. 8.
Judge’s injury will create further scrutiny as to whether he should have gone on a rehab assignment instead of coming straight back into games. The captain was adamant about not wanting to waste time playing in minor league games, and the Yankees – who could not force Judge to go on a rehab assignment – tried to ease him back in carefully. They played him for six innings his first game back – much to his chagrin – then eight innings, then an off day. Judge then played four straight games through Monday’s playoff clincher before the Yankees sat him again on Tuesday, after which they were hopeful he would essentially be a full go.
But then came the nightmare, when Judge felt some calf tightness while playing the field in the bottom of the first inning and then by the top of the sixth, was pinch hit for by Heliot Ramos.
Before the injury, Judge was still trying to lock in his timing at the plate after a long layoff, batting 4-for-23 (.174) with a .513 OPS and one home run. These final three series were supposed to be about getting him in a good spot for the postseason, but now he will spend them getting treatment and rehabbing in hopes of playing again.
Fellow Yankees slugger Giancarlo Stanton suffered a calf strain in late April and has not played another game since, though he was initially on the verge of a return in June before suffering two more calf strains since.
Judge, after leaving Wednesday’s game against the Twins early, likened the issue to something he would deal with in spring training while building up his workload, except it is now September.
In the meantime, the Yankees started Ramos in right field on Friday against Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodríguez, and he will likely get the majority of the time there down the stretch.
Even before Judge’s injury, the Yankees were already dealing with a few players trying to make a comeback in time for the playoffs, including Jazz Chisholm Jr. (right thumb sprain), Trent Grisham (right hamstring strain) and Ryan Weathers (left forearm flexor strain). Grisham, who could be ready by next week, now has a potential lane to come back in center field, bumping Spencer Jones to right. Chisholm is also expected to be activated when the Yankees return home.
Max Schuemann will join the Yankees on Saturday to take Judge’s roster spot.
“We’re gonna have to find a way,” Cody Bellinger said. “I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself, and I’m fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win and beat anybody.”

Aaron Judge, tres veces Jugador Más Valioso (MVP) de la Liga Americana, se perderá la mayor parte o quizá el resto de la temporada regular después de que los Yankees de Nueva York anunciaron el viernes que lo colocarán en la lista de lesionados de 10 días debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha.

Judge fue retirado por un bateador emergente en la sexta entrada el miércoles durante un juego contra los Mellizos de Minnesota debido a las molestias en la pierna. En ese momento, señaló que se trataba de una medida de precaución.
Judge bateó de 26-4, con 13 ponches y un extrabase, en siete juegos desde que regresó la semana pasada tras una fractura de costilla, lesión que lo mantuvo fuera de la alineación durante más de tres meses.

So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air. New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday. New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster. After New York clinched a pl
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could make a surprising move on Anthony Volpe.
Volpe has had success since being recalled, but George Lombard Jr. has taken over as the starting shortstop. So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air.
New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.
New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision
Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.
After New York clinched a playoff spot, Yankees analysts Bryan Hoch and Patrick Donnelly of MLB.com revealed the likely playoff roster, and they didn't have Volpe on it.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Aaron Judge, Heliot Ramos
DH: Ben Rice
SP: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
RP: David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren
The Yankees leaving Volpe off the playoff roster would be a disappointing outcome for the shortstop. It also could signal the end of his tenure in New York as Lombard is the shortstop of the future.
Volpe is hitting .253 with 2 home runs and 26 RBIs this season with the Yankees.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
However, despite clinching a playoff spot, the Yankees made it clear the job isn't finished. New York likely won't win the AL East again, which is frustrating, but the Yankees have confidence they can go on a deep playoff run.
The Yankees are 88-64 and 5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the AL East.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Anthony Volpe Handed Harsh Take on New York Yankees Future Before Playoffs appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees’ Aaron Judge returning to IL with right calf strain
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips

While an official move hasn’t been made yet, multiple sources told the Daily News that utilityman Max Schuemann will be recalled from Triple-A to take Judge’s place. Judge, now ineligible to return until the final game of the regular season, suffered what the Yankees initially called a right lower leg injury during the t
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Aaron Judge is going back on the shelf.
The Yankees’ captain will be placed on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain on Saturday, the team announced Friday. While an official move hasn’t been made yet, multiple sources told the Daily News that utilityman Max Schuemann will be recalled from Triple-A to take Judge’s place.
Judge, now ineligible to return until the final game of the regular season, suffered what the Yankees initially called a right lower leg injury during the team’s extra-inning loss to the Twins on Wednesday. The slugger said he first felt something while playing the field in the first inning, but he didn’t exit the game until Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him in the sixth inning.
Judge could be seen grimacing on a check swing during the third inning and hobbling in the outfield during the fifth inning. Aaron Boone said he wasn’t made of Judge’s injury until just before the right fielder was pulled from the game; the skipper noticed the hobbling during the fifth frame.
“I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said Wednesday. “But in talking it over, I thought it’d be the right move to come out so we don’t cost the team in the field or on the basepaths.
“I didn’t think it was smart to push it too much here.”
Judge’s return to the IL comes with him just seven games removed from a 99-day absence for a stress fracture in his first right rib. That injury sidelined him from May 31 through Sept. 7.
On Wednesday, Judge, 4-for-23 (.174) with one home run and three RBI since coming back, compared his new injury to the types of nagging issues that pop up during spring training and at the start of the season when players start ramping up their bodies. He has been doing just that since returning from his rib injury on Sept. 8.
“We’re still trying to ramp up, so there’s going to be little things like this that come up,” said Judge, who got his wish and skipped a rehab assignment for his rib.
Judge also only faced live pitching once before returning from his rib injury. He did not play in full games his first two days back, and he had off on Sept. 10 and Sept. 15.
Asked on Wednesday if his new injury made him rethink his rehab process, Judge told The News, “People blow out their calves and blow out their quads in rehab assignments, so I don’t think taking a game in Double-A will change any of that.”
He added that he felt his build-up has been gradual, as he had felt asymptomatic for weeks before returning.
“That’s what we kind of did with playing the [seven] innings, playing the eight innings,” Judge said, referring to his planned early exits in his first two games back, the first of which he said he was “not happy” about the night of.
The Yankees had one of the worst offenses in baseball during Judge’s last IL stint, ranking last in K% (26.1%); 29th in wRC+ (90) and average (.227); 28th in wOBA (.299); 27th in OPS (.681); and 24th in runs scored (341) from June 2 through Sept. 7.
Judge’s latest IL stint also comes with just 10 games remaining in the regular season. That was prior to beginning a three-game series at Arizona’s Chase Field on Friday. The second-place Yanks, who have already secured a playoff berth, will then host a highly-anticipated four-game series against the division-leading Rays from Sept. 22-24.
Now they’ll play those games without their best player, worsening the Bombers’ already-unlikely odds of snatching a division title from Tampa Bay.

"I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said on Wednesday. “But kind of talking it over, I thought it'd be the right move to come out, so I don't cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepath.”

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge Injured, Latest Updates on Yankees Star's Timeline to Return Ahead of 2026 MLB Playoffs
Just over a week after he returned from a rib injury that kept him out for most of the season, Aaron Judge is heading back to the injured list.
Judge is being placed on the 10-day IL with a calf strain, the New York Yankees announced Friday.
TOP NEWS
Mets 1B Has Memory Loss After Collision
Mets player calls out own fans
Ichiro Throws CRAZY Shutout 🔱
Judge left Wednesday's game against the Minnesota Twins in the sixth inning because of right lower leg tightness. He said after the game that he felt something during the first inning and eventually decided he should come out.
Judge went 0-for-2 with a pair of strikeouts before he exited the game. Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him.
Judge suffered a rib injury in late May and missed more than three months of action, finally making his return last Tuesday against the Colorado Rockies. Since returning, he's gone 4-for-21 with a home run and three RBI, clearly still working his way back to 100 percent.
After his return, the three-time AL MVP addressed having to get back into shape while simultaneously helping the Yankees fight for ideal playoff seeding.
"I get paid to do this, so I gotta go do it," Judge told reporters. "That's the end of it. I get paid to go out there and give my best to the New York Yankees and these fans. So, you get paid to win games so you gotta keep going out there and winning games."
Luckily for Judge, New York managed to stay afloat during his absence. The Yankees are sitting in second place in the AL East and secured a spot in the postseason earlier this week.
The Bronx Bombers are six games ahead of the Boston Red Sox and should be able to secure the top wild-card spot.
Even though New York has guaranteed a spot in the playoffs, Judge's injury is worrisome. The Yankees may have managed when he was gone, but making a World Series push without their star would be a different story.
With Judge heading back to the injured list, the Yankees will hope their star slugger can return to the lineup sooner rather than later as New York battles for playoff position in the AL East.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Aaron Judge to hit IL due to calf strain, can't return until Yankees' final game of regular season

Of course, it's unclear if he will be ready to play by then. Per Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News, the Yankees plan to call up outfielder
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees star Aaron Judge will be placed on the 10-day injured list due to a right calf strain, the club announced Friday.
Assuming the roster move is backdated to Thursday, the day after Judge's last on-field appearance, the three-time AL MVP won't be eligible to return until Sept. 27, the day of the Yankees' final game of the regular season. Of course, it's unclear if he will be ready to play by then.
Per Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News, the Yankees plan to call up outfielder Max Schuemann from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre as the corresponding move for Judge.
Judge came off the IL only 10 days earlier after missing three months due to a stress fracture in his ribs. He has played in seven games since then, going 4-for-23 with 1 homer and 13 strikeouts.
This injury popped up on Wednesday, when Judge left a game due to what he described as stiffness in his lower right leg. Per MLB.com, Judge didn't point to any one play causing the issue. Rather, he described it as the kind of issue that arises after a long layoff like his IL stint:
"I feel like you deal with this every spring training. You know, usually at the start of the season once you start ramping up again, things pop up, and that's where we've been," Judge said. "Thankfully, this whole time coming back, nothing's really nagged us. So hopefully it's just one little thing and then we're back out there soon."
Unfortunately, the injury appears to not be one little thing.
Judge has won AL MVP in three of the past four seasons, but this year has not gone according to plan. He got off to a slow start by his standards, slashing only .248/.375/.533 until the Yankees placed him on the IL in early June. Those struggles were partially due to the rib injury, which he reportedly tried to play through for six weeks.
Judge didn't return to the lineup until Sept. 8, and now he's going back on the shelf. Going forward, he represents an enormous unknown for the Yankees, who sit second in the AL East at 88-64. They are currently on pace for a second straight wild-card series clash with the Boston Red Sox.
At best, Judge could return right before the playoffs. At worst, he might have already played his final game of 2026.
Not counting his cup of coffee in 2016 or the COVID-shortened 2020 season, Judge has never played in fewer than the 66 games he's seen in 2026 or posted an OPS+ lower than this year's 140 (which is still very good). That adds up to a career-worst season for Judge at 34 years old.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees' Aaron Judge Dilemma Features a Problem No One is Discussing
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge returned from a rib stress fracture on Sept. 8, and it took him all of seven games to get injured again. Judge left Wednesday's loss to the Minnesota Twins as a result of what he and the team are calling a "lower leg injury," which almost surely means a calf issue. There have been no definitive updates on his status since, and it's looking more and more like Judge will not play against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday night. The playoffs start on Sept. 2
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge returned from a rib stress fracture on Sept. 8, and it took him all of seven games to get injured again.
Judge left Wednesday's loss to the Minnesota Twins as a result of what he and the team are calling a "lower leg injury," which almost surely means a calf issue.
There have been no definitive updates on his status since, and it's looking more and more like Judge will not play against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday night.
The playoffs start on Sept. 29, which obviously creates a nightmare scenario for the Yankees. Even if Judge is healthy enough to play.
Why? Because at this point, the three-time AL MVP pretty much has to serve as a designated hitter. Unless Judge has a minor bruise in his calf, it seems highly unlikely that he will be able to play right field if he returns.
Why is that a big deal? Because it completely messes up New York's lineup.
The Yankees acquired Luis Garcia Jr. back at the MLB trade deadline with the expectation that he would be the first baseman. Ben Rice would then serve as DH, as Giancarlo Stanton's status was up in the air then, and now, it looks like Stanton is done for the year.
When Judge is in right field, that isn't an issue. Garcia plays first, Rice goes to DH and all three of those big boppers are in the lineup.
But with Judge potentially having to spend all of his time at designated hitter, that means Garcia would almost certainly get the boot.
You're not platooning Rice and Garcia at first. They're both lefties, and you always want Rice's bat in the lineup no matter what. What the Yankees could have done was platoon Garcia and Paul Goldschmidt at first base given how much Goldschmidt mashes lefties, but if Judge is DHing, that isn't possible.
If Judge is healthy enough to hit, he'll obviously be in the lineup. Running the bases could be another story (just ask Giancarlo), but the more you limit Judge's movement, the better.
That the Yankees have been so mum on Judge's status is concerning. If there weren't a major problem here, they surely would have already said something.
And after all of the experience fans have had with the medical stuff and how New York handles injuries, they know by now that when there is silence, there is reason to worry.
Hopefully, Judge's malady is no big deal and he can head back out to right field within the next week. But Yankees fans need to prepare for other scenarios, and even if Judge does return, that could mean their lineup still wouldn't be all it could be,

item.title: [MLB.com] ¿Cómo responderán los jóvenes de Yankees en los playoffs?
item.dc:creator: Patrick Donnelly
item.description: Es común pensar en los Yankees como un equipo experimentado en los playoffs. Después de todo, ésta es la octava vez en nueve años que han llegado a la postemporada bajo la dirección del manager Aaron Boone. Y una rápida mirada a algunos de sus jugadores principales muestra una alineación que varía entre un poco y una gran cantidad de experiencia en octubre. Jugador, Número de Partidos de Playoffs de por vida Cody Bellinger, 76 Aaron Judge, 65 Paul Goldschmidt, 29 Trent Grisham, 26 Jazz Chisholm,
item.content:encoded:
Es común pensar en los Yankees como un equipo experimentado en los playoffs. Después de todo, ésta es la octava vez en nueve años que han llegado a la postemporada bajo la dirección del manager Aaron Boone. Y una rápida mirada a algunos de sus jugadores principales muestra una alineación que varía entre un poco y una gran cantidad de experiencia en octubre.
Jugador, Número de Partidos de Playoffs de por vida
Cody Bellinger, 76
Aaron Judge, 65
Paul Goldschmidt, 29
Trent Grisham, 26
Jazz Chisholm, Jr. 24
Austin Wells, 21
Anthony Volpe, 21
Amed Rosario, 11
Ryan McMahon, 10
Ben Rice, 6
José Caballero, 3
Pero faltan algunos nombres en esa lista: El campocorto George Lombard Jr., el jardinero Spencer Jones, el primera base dominicano Luis García Jr. y el jardinero puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos. Ninguno de esos cuatro nunca ha jugado en la postemporada, ya sea con los Yankees o, como es el caso de García y Ramos, con sus equipos anteriores.
Ahora, es posible que algunos de los jugadores veteranos lesionados -- Grisham y Chisholm, específicamente -- puedan regresar a la alineación y enviar a algunos de esos nuevos rostros a la banca o fuera del roster de postemporada por completo. Pero es seguro decir que los Yankees van a contar con al menos algunos novatos en los playoffs el próximo mes, en su búsqueda de ganar su primera Serie Mundial desde el 2009.
Boone ha expresado que sus jóvenes y los recién llegados a los playoffs tienen otra ventaja sobre los jugadores en otros mercados.
"Jugar para los Yankees, jugar en Nueva York”, dijo, "tiene una manera de prepararte para la postemporada”.
Éste ha sido un año de transición en las Grandes Ligas. Consulta la primera ronda del Draft del 2023 si quieres pruebas. No menos de 19 de las 37 selecciones de primera ronda y de compensación han debutado en las Mayores, y muchos de ellos ya son jugadores clave en sus equipos.
"Los jugadores están llegando a las Grandes Ligas a un ritmo muy rápido ahora y a temprana edad”, manifestó el piloto de los Tigers, A.J. Hinch, quien ha dado la bienvenida a la tercera selección Max Clark y al favorito para Novato del Año de la Liga Americana, Kevin McGonigle, a Detroit este año. "No creo que se sientan tan impresionados por los grandes pasos que están dando”.
Para los Yankees, ese grupo incluye a Lombard, quien se ha aclimatado bien desde que fue subido a principios de agosto. Y Jones fue elogiado recientemente nada menos que por Aaron Judge, quien dijo que el jardinero novato "realmente ha evolucionado cada vez que ha sido subido, mejorando un poco más en cada ocasión”.
Por supuesto, habrá contratiempos en el camino. El miércoles, Jones se fue de 6-0 con cinco ponches y cometió un error cuando dejó caer un batazo en el jardín central. Y Lombard no pudo atrapar un roletazo del boricua Victor Caratini en la 13ª entrada que fue considerado un sencillo mientras los Mellizos vencían a los Yankees.
Pero cualquiera que siga el béisbol sabe que los días malos y las malas jugadas son parte del ciclo de crecimiento de un jugador de Grandes Ligas. La clave es aprender de ellos para poder limitarlos en el futuro. Y todo ello -- lo bueno, lo malo y lo ocasionalmente feo -- ayuda a preparar a un joven jugador para su primera vez jugando en el béisbol de octubre.
El mundo está a punto de descubrir lo preparados que están los Yankees jóvenes. Pero Jones ofreció un poco de tranquilidad el lunes mientras disfrutaba de la celebración en el vestuario después de la victoria en Target Field que aseguró otra clasificación de Nueva York para los playoffs.
"Creo que para nosotros, jugamos mejor cuando la multitud se vuelve más ruidosa", dijo. "Estoy bien emocionado por lo que está por venir”.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yankees Announce Starting Pitchers for Diamondbacks Series: Gerrit Cole Must Get Back on Track

item.description: If there's one reason to think the New York Yankees have a minuscule chance of overcoming a five-game deficit in the American League East, it's the probable pitchers every series. item.content:encoded:
If there's one reason to think the New York Yankees have a minuscule chance of overcoming a five-game deficit in the American League East, it's the probable pitchers every series. Aaron Boone's Bombers can feature one of his many frontline starters on a given night, and in this series against the Arizona Diamondbacks, two of his four best pitchers take the mound.
On paper, you see the first two starters and think the advantage should go to the Yankees, but one issue in particular has hampered their former Cy Young winner. If this team is going to make any noise in the postseason, he'll have to work on it, and it starts with this series.
Friday, Sept. 18 (9:40 p.m. ET): Gerrit Cole (NYY) vs. Eduardo Rodriguez (ARI)
Eduardo Rodriguez has proven to be a playoff-caliber pitcher, and his 2.62 ERA in 178.1 IP is frontline stuff. He is the type of high-level arm they'll see in the postseason. Rodriguez typically pitches to contact, holding opposing batters to an 87.3 MPH average exit velocity and a 33% hard-hit rate. This can be one of those games where the Yankees hit ground balls against him for 7+ innings.
Cole, meanwhile, has been snakebit by the long ball, and it isn't so wild to say that the advantage could go to Rodriguez in this one if Cole pitches the way he has. It's been a concerning turn of events ever since that game against the San Diego Padres. For now, the advantage goes to Rodriguez, who'll want to harken back to his Boston days and shut down the Yankees.
Saturday, Sept. 19 (8:10 p.m. ET): Cam Schlittler (NYY) vs. Brandon Pfadt (ARI)
Pfaadt, though, isn't a slouch by any means, and if the Yankees are going to be without Aaron Judge — which usually means the offense will be listless — what can be said about Rodriguez applies to Pfaadt here.
The 27-year-old Arizona starter has a 68th-percentile groundball rate and holds hitters to a 35.5% hard-hit rate. It could be another instance of the Yankees hitting a ton of ground balls. Most competent offenses should be able to hold their own, but it's hard to trust the Yankees 1-through-9 these days. They might need a great pitching performance by Schlittler and win one of those 2-0 or 3-0 games here.
Pfaadt has one of the best walk rates in baseball. His 5.7% BB% is in the 91st percentile, so he'll force them to make contact, and that can be a recipe for disaster for a team that can't put together runs.
Sunday, Sept. 20 (4:10 p.m. ET): Will Warren (NYY) vs. Corbin Burnes (ARI)
Corbin Burnes has pitched all of 7.2 innings this season. He's coming back from Tommy John surgery, which he had last June. It feels like a quick recovery, and he'll likely be on a pitch limit. That said, the sooner the Yankees can get him back in the game, the better.
Every Warren start can't be a high-scoring affair because he can be brilliant or a disaster, so hopefully they get a brilliant Warren here while also chasing Burnes out of the game quickly. If he's out by the third, they can ground down that bullpen.
Warren is coming off a solid outing against the Twins earlier this week, where he allowed five hits, two runs (zero earned), two walks, and racked up six strikeouts in 5.2 innings.
The advantage should go to the Yankees if Warren gives them length, but again, as with any game, it will come down to whether they can score.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Cody Bellinger Soluciona Un Problema Clave De Los Yankees Que Lastraba Su Alineación Para La Serie Mundial De 2024
item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — La diferencia de tres puntos de Cody Bellinger en el platoon le da a los Yankees una gran ventaja en la alineación para la postemporada de octubre.
Con un balance de 88-64, los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero siguen a cinco partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan 10 partidos de la temporada regular. La clasificación sigue siendo importante. Y también lo es una alineación que tendrá poco margen de error cuando los rivales puedan adaptar sus estrategias de pitcheo para contrarrestarla.
Ahí es donde la postemporada de 2024 sigue siendo un contexto útil. Nueva York llegó a la Serie Mundial antes de caer ante los Dodgers en cinco partidos, pero el jardín izquierdo nunca llegó a ser una fuente fiable de producción tanto ofensiva como defensiva. Alex Verdugo terminó esa temporada regular con un promedio de .233/.291/.356 y un OPS+ de 83, y luego bateó .208/.309/.313 con un OPS de .622 en 14 partidos de postemporada.
El problema duró más de un mes de octubre. Tras la última temporada de Brett Gardner con los Yankees en 2021, el jardín izquierdo pasó a ser una posición rotativa en lugar de un punto fuerte consolidado. Las estadísticas posicionales de FanGraphs sitúan al jardín izquierdo de los Yankees en solo 1,6 fWAR entre 2021 y 2024, lo que lo coloca en el puesto 28 de las Grandes Ligas en ese periodo. Esa trayectoria dejó a Nueva York buscando tanto rendimiento como estabilidad, en lugar de otro parche de una sola temporada en una posición defensiva clave. Por fin, la situación parece haber cambiado.
Bellinger convierte el jardín izquierdo de un compromiso en un punto fuerte
Cody Bellinger es la razón más clara. El miércoles conectó 3 de 5, con una base por bolas, una carrera y una base robada, lo que le ha permitido sumar varios hits en cinco de sus últimos siete partidos. Su racha va más allá de unas cuantas noches de septiembre.
Bellinger ha bateado .340 con cinco jonrones, 18 carreras impulsadas y un wRC+ de 148 en 23 partidos desde que volvió el 23 de agosto tras una distensión de grado 2 en el isquiotibial izquierdo. Al comenzar el viernes, llevaba un promedio de bateo de .276/.351/.444, con 16 jonrones y 71 carreras impulsadas en 125 partidos.
Los Yankees acabaron con un balance de 15-7 en los primeros 22 partidos tras su regreso, batearon .274/.336/.440 como equipo, registraron un diferencial de carreras de +42 y anotaron al menos cinco carreras en 14 ocasiones. Llegaron a las seis carreras en 12 ocasiones y a las siete en nueve. Bellinger ha aportado toda esa potencia ofensiva sin dejar de ser un defensor decisivo.
Sports Info Solutions le atribuye a Bellinger 20 carreras defensivas salvadas en el jardín izquierdo, mientras que Statcast le da seis outs por encima de la media en todo el jardín. Ese valor en ambos aspectos es la diferencia clave con respecto a 2024, y su capacidad para jugar tanto en el jardín central como en primera base aporta a los Yankees una mayor flexibilidad en la plantilla.
Una derrota aplastante dejó claro por qué su bate es tan importante
Los Yankees pudieron comprobar su poder ofensivo durante la derrota por 12-2 ante los Mets el 12 de septiembre en el Yankee Stadium. Bellinger anotó las dos carreras de Nueva York con un sencillo impulsador en la cuarta entrada y un jonrón solitario en la sexta. Era su tercer jonrón en cuatro partidos en ese momento.
Aaron Boone estaba explicando por qué el lanzador titular de los Mets, Zac Thornton, había controlado al resto de la alineación. Ese comentario ponía de manifiesto lo poco que Cody Bellinger había recibido ayuda aquella tarde.
«Está claro que se puso por delante ahí y sus lanzamientos a la zona de strike fueron realmente buenos», dijo Boone.
Desde entonces, el promedio de bateo de Bellinger en septiembre ha subido hasta el 0,390 en 14 partidos, con cuatro jonrones, 12 carreras impulsadas y 14 carreras anotadas. Los Yankees han necesitado esa estabilidad mientras otras partes de la alineación han tenido que adaptarse a las lesiones y a los enfrentamientos.
Una diferencia de tres puntos en el platoon cambia las cuentas de octubre
Quizá la cifra más reveladora sea la que apenas varía. Hasta el miércoles, Bellinger tiene un OPS de 0,797 contra lanzadores zurdos y un OPS de 0,794 contra lanzadores diestros. Esa diferencia de tres puntos le da a los Yankees un bateador en el centro del orden de bateo que no hace falta ocultar cuando los rivales cambian de lanzador.
El panorama del platooning de los Yankees también sitúa a Aaron Judge y Ben Rice entre sus bateadores titulares más equilibrados. Bellinger es otro bateador que puede quedarse en el partido sin que Boone tenga que sacrificar el ataque por la defensa ni la defensa por el ataque, una cualidad muy valiosa cuando, en octubre, los bullpens cambian los enfrentamientos inning tras inning.
El precio original del traspaso solo cuenta la mitad de la historia
Los Yankees ficharon a Bellinger de los Cubs en diciembre de 2024 a cambio del lanzador diestro Cody Poteet, y Chicago también aportó 5 millones de dólares. El precio de ese traspaso sigue siendo impresionante, pero no es el coste total. Después de que Bellinger se convirtiera en agente libre, Nueva York lo volvió a fichar en enero con un contrato de cinco años y 162,5 millones de dólares.
En 2025, sumó 29 jonrones, 98 carreras impulsadas y 4,9 fWAR. El valor que le da FanGraphs para 2026 ronda ahora los cuatro fWAR. Según un cálculo basado en sus estadísticas totales de la MLB durante las dos temporadas con los Yankees , se sitúa en 45 jonrones, 169 carreras impulsadas y un promedio de bateo combinado de aproximadamente .274/.341/.464.
Con la clasificación para la postemporada asegurada y la División Este de la Liga Americana aún en juego, a los Yankees les quedan 10 partidos para pulir su alineación de octubre. El reciente repunte de Bellinger, su rendimiento casi idéntico en el plato y su defensa en el jardín izquierdo aportan a Nueva York algo que su equipo de la Serie Mundial de 2024 nunca tuvo de forma constante en esa posición: un titular que puede seguir formando parte del plan independientemente del rival.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.content:encoded:
The two most valuable Yankees this season are a starting pitcher named Cam Schlittler, from Walpole, Mass., and Northeastern University, a school within walking distance of Fenway Park, and Ben Rice, who comes out of Cohasset, Mass., on the state’s South Shore, about 30 miles from Fenway. If the Yankees are hosting a Wild Card Series against the Red Sox in less than two weeks -- at Yankee Stadium and not Fenway -- Schlittler and Rice will be the biggest reasons.
Schlittler ought to win the AL Cy Young Award and ought to be an MVP candidate for the whole league. David Cone, now a Yankees broadcaster for the YES network and once a great Yankee himself, has one word to describe what he’s seen from Schlittler this season:
“Nails.”
Here’s a breakdown of Schlittler’s ERA, month by month after one start in March, when, of course, he threw a shutout (eight strikeouts) into the sixth inning against the Giants:
1.73 in April
1.48 in May
3.38 in June
1.93 in July
2.33 in August
0.86 so far in September
Carlos Rodón got hurt. Max Fried got hurt. Gerrit Cole joined the season late, and he hasn’t looked like his own Cy Young self lately. It is been Schlittler who has been the Yankees' ace, who is their Game 1 guy, who has carried the staff. He is not going to end up with a 25-3 record and an ERA of 1.74 the way Ron Guidry did nearly 50 years ago. But Schlittler is at 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA going into his last few starts of the regular season. He has been the first young power starter out of the Yankees’ system since Guidry to be this good, and this dominant.
But Rice has been just as important to their offense.
In a season when Aaron Judge was gone for more than 80 games because of a fracture to his rib cage. Then, after Judge finally got back into the lineup and even hit his first home run in months, he left a game against the Twins the other day because of pain in his lower leg. It is why you have to believe, if and when Judge is back in the lineup again, he’s going to be a swing and a prayer the rest of the way.
So No. 99 went away. So did Cody Bellinger, the Yankees’ second-most important hitter a year ago, before he finally returned from the IL. But even when the Yankees struggled to score runs, and even in a roller-coaster year that saw Rice hit just .196 in June and .184 in August, it is Rice who has been the Yankees' hitting star, coming into a weekend series against the Diamondbacks with 38 home runs and still with a chance to knock in 100.
Luis García Jr. showed up from the Nationals at the Trade Deadline to give him some backup. Bellinger has been on a heater since coming off the IL, with five homers, 18 RBIs and a .344 average over his last 22 games. But it was Rice around whom the Yankees built what offense they had before all that, while they were staying ahead of the Red Sox and at least maintaining contact with the Rays.
You know how many homegrown Yankees have hit 40 or more home runs in a season in the last 75 years? Two. One was named Mickey Mantle and the other is Judge. There have been other Yankees sluggers who got to 40 and beyond. Alex Rodriguez once made it all the way to 57. But they all came from somewhere else. Rice is the same as Schlittler: He hasn’t just come to this moment from New England, he’s someone the Yankees drafted in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft (Schlittler was out of the seventh round the following year).
Alfonso Soriano made his own run at 40 more than 20 years ago. Did it twice. But Soriano came to the Yankees as a free agent from Japan. So think about the company Rice will be keeping if does get to 40 homers, starting with his chance this weekend against the Diamondbacks:
Mantle. Judge.
Here is something Rice’s manager, Aaron Boone, has said about him:
"I got my first taste of him in Spring Training of '24, and it was like, 'Oh, OK.' But then this year, it's gone to even another level.”
Here is something else:
“I think he's turning into one of the best hitters in the league."
Rice himself has predictably low-keyed what he’s done for the Yankees so far.
"The year is still in progress, you know?” he said. “It's still going on. We've got more games to play and a long road ahead, so I can't really look back and assess it fully yet."
It really has been a roller-coaster ride occasionally. He has struggled occasionally against left-handed pitchers, but his season-long average against them stands at .254 with 10 home runs and 29 RBIs.
We know what Schlittler’s numbers are. Rice’s, though, can get a little lost sometimes. But in a year where he’s batted everywhere from leadoff to cleanup, when Judge was gone for more than half the time, he has been indispensable, too. And still has a shot to be a 40-homer guy for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Baseball legend Mariano Rivera on Yankees '90s Dynasty, Core 4, pressure of playing in NYC and his new Mo's Hot Sauce appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
When the ninth inning arrived in the Bronx, nothing was more intimidating for opposing hitters than Mariano Rivera jogging out of the bullpen with his iconic "Enter Sandman" entrance music playing. Over 19 seasons with the New York Yankees, Rivera established himself as the greatest closer of all time, retiring as MLB's career leader with 652 saves. The first player ever unanimously elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame, Rivera was at his best when the stakes were highest, helping anchor a Yankees dynasty that won five World Series championships during his career.
From his virtually unhittable cutter to his unmatched composure in October, Rivera became synonymous with dominance in the ninth inning. He recorded an MLB-record 42 postseason saves and a remarkable 0.70 ERA across 141 playoff innings, playing an integral role alongside Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, and Jorge Posada in a homegrown group that became known as the Yankees' "Core Four."
Baseball legend Mariano Rivera with ClutchPoints' Rob Lepelstat for an exclusive interview in the Bronx, NY – just minutes from Yankee Stadium, where Mo spent his entire 19-year MLB career with the Yankees
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
More than a decade after throwing his final pitch, Rivera's impact continues to extend beyond the mound. The Yankees legend has entered the hot sauce business with Mo's Heat, his new hot sauce brand that gives Rivera an opportunity to bring his competitive mentality into a completely different arena while connecting with fans in a new way.
During an exclusive interview with ClutchPoints' Rob Lepelstat, Rivera discussed the inspiration behind Mo's Hot Sauce, revealed the mentality that allowed him to thrive in baseball's biggest moments, reflected on the Yankees' iconic 1990s dynasty and his relationship with the Core Four, opened up about playing alongside "The Captain" Derek Jeter, and shared his advice for today's Yankees as they attempt to bring a 28th World Series championship to the Bronx.
Mo's Hot Sauce
Baseball legend Mariano Rivera made a career out of bringing the heat in the ninth inning. Now, the legendary New York Yankees closer is doing it in a much different way.
Rivera has entered the hot sauce business with Mo's Hot Sauce, adding another venture to a résumé that already includes five World Series championships, a unanimous Baseball Hall of Fame induction, MLB's all-time saves record (652) and recognition as the greatest closer in the history of the sport.
Mariano is proud of his roots, which is why Mo's Heat features authentic Panamanian flavors, hand-selected habanero peppers, and all-natural ingredients from their 122-year-old hot sauce recipe.
It includes three flavors: The Sinker, The Curve and the signature sauce, The Cutter (of course!), named after Rivera's unhittable pitch.
The venture is about more than simply putting his famous name on a bottle. He explained the motivation behind Mo's Hot Sauce and why he believes the product can stand out in a crowded market.
"This product is something special for me, dear to my heart, so I'm happy that we could come up with this," Rivera described. "It's all what you put in there, you know? Besides the ingredients, you have to put love and passion in there, you know, commitment. And—and that's what we have done. You know, besides all the ingredients that are in there, all-natural, by the way, I mean, we're putting a lot of effort, a lot of passion, love, and commitment to make sure that the fans and people love this sauce. Not because Mariano, but because of the sauce."
From the Mo's Heat website: Made with highly selected habanero peppers and spices using a 122-year-old recipe, Mo's Heat hot sauces offer a unique flavor and aroma to enhance any meal. As an MLB pitcher, Mariano Rivera played every game for his home country, Panama. And he founded Mo's Heat to celebrate their flavor, character, and fire.
Fans can find out more information, including where to buy, pricing, and flavors, at https://mosheatsauces.com/.
The Closer Mentality
When the Yankees needed three outs to close out a game, there was nobody they trusted more than Rivera.
The numbers speak for themselves. Rivera finished his career as MLB's all-time saves leader with 652, but his dominance became even more pronounced when the lights were brightest. In 96 postseason appearances, Rivera recorded 42 saves while allowing just 11 earned runs, good for the lowest ERA in playoff history (0.70).
Yet Rivera's greatness wasn't simply the product of his famous cutter. His ability to remain calm in moments that could overwhelm even the best players became as much a part of his reputation as the pitch itself.
Rivera explained how he approached those pressure-packed situations and what allowed him to maintain the same mentality whether he was pitching in a regular-season game or trying to record the final outs of a World Series.
"I tried to simplify the game, I tried to simplify the way I pitch… If I can get you out in one pitch, I would try to do that. I wasn't afraid of contact."
That mindset helped Rivera become synonymous with the closer position and gave the Yankees an enormous advantage during their championship years: When No. 42 entered the game, everyone in the ballpark knew exactly what was coming — and hitters still struggled to stop it.
Rivera's Cutter
Few weapons in sports history carry the mythic status of Mariano Rivera's cut fastball. Thrown with effortless arm speed and late, violent movement, the pitch shattered hundreds of bats—and just as many opposing rallies—en route to a record 652 career saves, and five World Series rings.
Hitters across Major League Baseball spent nearly two decades studying tape, anticipating the pitch, and bracing for it, yet virtually none could solve it. Ironically, the most unhittable pitch in baseball history wasn't engineered in a lab or perfected through endless trial and error; it was a divine accident that Rivera discovered while trying to do the exact opposite.
Rivcera's cutter came out of the exact same arm slot and had the same visual spin as his standard fastball. Batters had only roughly 0.17 seconds to react and could not tell the difference until it was too late.
The ball traveled at up to 90–95 mph and would break sharply by up to 8 inches, usually in the final 10 feet before reaching the plate.
Rivera threw the cutter roughly 88% of the time later in his career, per MLB.com. Hitters knew it was coming for nearly two decades, yet they still could not hit it.
When asked about the origin of his signature weapon, the Hall of Fame closer reflected on how a frustrating bullpen session with pitching coach Mel Stottlemyre ultimately gave birth to baseball perfection.
"It was God-given for sure, because we were trying to stop it from moving… I told [Mel Stottlemyre], 'Hey man, whatever's gonna happen is gonna happen, because I have no control of this pitch, let's leave it.'
The rest is history.
The Yankees' 1990s Dynasty
The Yankees' championship run of the late 1990s remains one of the greatest stretches by any team in modern baseball history.
After winning the World Series in 1996, New York put together a historic 1998 season before completing a three-peat with championships in 1999 and 2000. Over a five-season span, the Yankees won four World Series titles and established a dynasty that has yet to be replicated in MLB since.
Rivera was there for all of it.
Before becoming the Yankees' closer, Rivera played a crucial setup role during the 1996 championship season. Once he took over the ninth inning, he became one of the foundational pieces of a team that seemingly expected to be playing deep into October every year.
Looking back on those teams, Rivera reflected on what made that group so successful and why the Yankees were able to consistently perform when the stakes were at their highest.
The championships featured countless memorable moments, but Rivera believes the culture surrounding those Yankees teams was just as important as the talent on the roster.
"There was a—a commitment and—and a passion and love with 25 players. Well, before was the—the owner, you know, Mr. George was amazing, and then uh the coaching staff that they put together, Joe and—and the rest of the play—the rest of the coaches. And then the players. You know, I mean, we were family, we were a team, we were family. And that makes a lot of difference. You know, we don't—we don't try to separate ourselves, we try to unify ourselves even tighter, tighter and tighter. And as results, we have four championships in five years."
The Core 4
As the Yankees continued winning, four homegrown players became constants in the Bronx: Rivera, Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, and Jorge Posada.
Eventually dubbed the "Core Four," the group came through the Yankees organization together before becoming central figures in one of the most successful eras in franchise history. Rivera, Jeter, Pettitte, and Posada were teammates for five World Series championships, with their careers becoming permanently intertwined in Yankees history.
What made the group unique wasn't simply its success. Each player filled a distinctly different role, yet all four shared the experience of growing from prospects into established stars while dealing with the expectations that came with playing in New York.
Rivera reflected on his relationship with Jeter, Pettitte, and Posada and what it meant to experience so much of his career alongside the same group of teammates.
"We're talking about family. We're not talking about teammates or players… We grew up together, coming from the minor league system all the way to the big leagues… We were just brainwashed: 'We need to win regardless.' It's not about second place, it's about winning the whole thing."
Years after their final game together, the Core Four remains synonymous with an era when October baseball in the Bronx felt almost inevitable.
The Captain, Derek Jeter
Within that Core Four, Rivera shared an especially remarkable journey with Derek Jeter.
Both made their MLB debuts in 1995. Neither could have known at the time that they would spend nearly two decades together and eventually become two of the most recognizable Yankees of their generation.
Jeter became the captain and face of the franchise. Rivera became the greatest closer in baseball history. Together, they were fixtures on five championship teams and experienced virtually everything the sport had to offer.
Their partnership also produced one of the most memorable moments of Rivera's final season. During his last appearance at Yankee Stadium in 2013, Jeter and Pettitte walked to the mound to remove an emotional Rivera from the game.
Rivera discussed what made Jeter such a special teammate and leader and what stood out about playing alongside him for so many years.
"Derek was the perfect captain because he had us… three players, teammates, that loved him and were willing to do whatever it takes to make him look good. He was the face, he had to be in the media talking about it, but we were all doing the job."
For all their individual accomplishments, their careers will forever be linked by what they accomplished together in pinstripes.
Rivera's Advice for Today's Yankees
More than a decade after Rivera threw his final pitch, the standard in the Bronx remains the same.
Winning games isn't enough. Making the postseason isn't enough. For the Yankees, success is ultimately measured in championships.
Rivera understands that pressure better than almost anyone. He experienced the expectations that came with wearing the pinstripes while playing for teams that didn't just reach October — they expected to win once they got there.
Today's Yankees face the challenge of creating their own championship legacy while playing under the weight of that history. Rivera offered his advice for the current roster and explained what it takes to succeed in New York when expectations are at their highest.
"They know the advice. It's just—just you have to push. You have to keep pushing and pushing and pushing to get it done, because I mean, this thing is not easy. People know that winning championships is not easy at all. So, we have the team, we have the players, so we just have to have the determination and the passion to get it done, you know? However, you have to get it done, you have to find a way to get it done, and that's what we're doing."
The names and faces have changed since Rivera's championship years, but the goal hasn't. For a franchise with 27 World Series titles, the winningest team in North American professional sports history, the expectation will always be to add another one.
—
Related: This bold Aaron Judge take may cause Yankees fans to raise eyebrows
Rob Lepelstat is an experienced sports media professional with over 7+ years in content creation, editorial, social media, reporting/interviewing, etc. His work has been featured in USA Today, Yahoo Sports, Bleacher Report, and more. Check out more of his interviews, including Jay-Z, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Lawrence Taylor, Ray Lewis, Derek Jeter, Ice Cube, "Dr. J" Julius Erving, Drew Brees, and Livvy Dunne here.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — La candidatura de Cam Schlittler al título de MVP ha reavivado una pregunta que es más antigua que la analítica, más antigua que la sala de vídeo. Incluso más antigua que la mayoría de los que ahora la debaten.
¿Qué significa realmente el valor? Un antiguo as de los Yankees ha vuelto a sacar a colación este debate esta semana, con un lanzador que casi nadie esperaba que entrara en la discusión.
La mayor parte del mundo del deporte se ha decantado por una división clara. Un trofeo para el mejor lanzador, otro para el mejor bateador. Los aficionados de los Yankees llevan más de una década viendo cómo los votantes se inclinan por esa opción.
¿Podrá Schlittler, de 25 años, romper con la tendencia?
Un experto nacional lo dejó muy claro. Analizó el panorama, dijo que la elección era obvia y señaló a un bateador potente de Houston. Según él, caso cerrado.
Pero alguien de los Yankees no estaba dispuesto a dejarlo zanjado tan fácilmente.
La primera temporada completa de Schlittler le ha valido el mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de todo el béisbol. David Cone, el exlanzador de los Yankees y actual comentarista, se mostró en desacuerdo con la idea de que el MVP de la Liga Americana sea pan comido. Su argumento no tenía que ver con las cifras, sino con la propia palabra.
Una fuente cercana dice que la elección es obvia
La crítica que recibió Cone vino de Ken Rosenthal, de The Athletic. En un vídeo que se publicó el 14 de septiembre, un día después de que Cam Schlittler lanzara seis entradas sin encajar ninguna carrera contra los Mets, Rosenthal reconoció los méritos del lanzador diestro antes de descartar su caso.
Rosenthal mencionó a Yordan Álvarez, de Houston, y a esa temporada ofensiva que los votantes suelen premiar, lo que contradice directamente el argumento de los Yankees. Álvarez llegaba a esta semana con un promedio de bateo de .310, 38 jonrones, 96 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de 1,016, mientras lucha por la Triple Corona de la Liga Americana.
«Yordan Álvarez, en mi opinión, parece la elección más obvia por lo que ha logrado en ataque», dijo Rosenthal.
Esa es la opinión generalizada. Y es precisamente la que Cone se propuso complicar.
Un grande de los Yankees le da un nuevo enfoque al tema
Cone defendió su postura en un programa del New York Post junto a Joel Sherman y Jon Heyman. En lugar de discutir las estadísticas, volvió a la prueba más antigua que ofrece el premio: la de la sustracción. ¿Qué pierde un equipo sin un jugador?
Cone planteó el ejercicio en general. Preguntó dónde estarían los Royals sin Bobby Witt Jr., dónde estarían los Astros sin Álvarez y dónde estarían los Yankees sin su as. En su opinión, eso situaba a Schlittler al mismo nivel que los bateadores.
«Si este año no contaran con Schlittler en los Yankees, ¿dónde estarían?», preguntó Cone. «Schlittler está entre los mejores. Sin duda, merece que se le tenga muy en cuenta».
Es un argumento de peso, teniendo en cuenta la temporada que han tenido los Yankees. Aaron Judge solo jugó 65 partidos por culpa de una lesión, y Gerrit Cole, Max Fried y Carlos Rodón también se perdieron partidos. En medio de toda esa agitación, Schlittler fue la constante al frente de la rotación, un lanzador titular en su primer año que llevó al equipo a luchar por el título.
El dato que le mantiene en la carrera
Este es el detalle que mantiene vivo el argumento de Cone, y que pocos medios han destacado. Bradford Doolittle, de ESPN, elabora un índice global llamado AXE, y en su análisis de premios de septiembre situó a Schlittler en segundo lugar entre todos los candidatos al MVP de la Liga Americana. Álvarez lideraba la clasificación con 146,9. Schlittler le seguía de cerca con 143,0.
No es una diferencia abismal. Es un empate casi perfecto en un modelo diseñado para combinar el lanzamiento y el bateo en una sola cifra, y mantiene al as de los Yankees en la lucha. Doolittle seguía diciendo que era una tarea difícil.
Las cifras lo explican todo. Doolittle describió una sucesión de acontecimientos casi perfecta. Schlittler probablemente necesitaría al menos una salida más, seguramente una larga en la que no encajara ninguna carrera, para hacerse con el título de mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas de las Grandes Ligas en solitario, en lugar de solo liderar la Liga Americana.
Ni siquiera un final impecable bastaría por sí solo. Álvarez también tendría que quedarse sin la Triple Corona mientras los Astros no se clasifican para los playoffs, y Junior Caminero, de Tampa Bay, necesitaría tener una última semana pésima que hiciera perder a los Rays el liderato de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Es una situación casi imposible, y por eso llama tanto la atención que Doolittle esté dispuesto a incluir a Schlittler en su clasificación.
Unas estadísticas que dan que hablar
Las cifras que lo acompañan explican por qué se le menciona. Schlittler tiene un balance de 14-6, con una ERA de 1,95, 228 strikeouts, un WHIP de 0,90 y un bWAR de 7,1 en 31 partidos como titular. Su marca de 1,95 le empata con Jacob Misiorowski, de Milwaukee, en la mejor ERA de la liga.
El contexto de los récords es aún más impresionante. Las 21 salidas de Schlittler en las que solo ha cedido una carrera o ninguna suponen un récord de los Yankees en una sola temporada, según Sarah Langs, de MLB.com. No se trata solo de un mes brillante. Son siete meses de control casi total por parte de un lanzador novato.
Últimamente ha estado aún mejor, con una ERA de 0,86 este mes, mientras supera las 180 entradas. Varios medios lo sitúan como líder de la Liga Americana en WAR de Baseball-Reference, la métrica exacta que mide el valor que describió Cone. Su ERA también se encuentra entre las más bajas de un lanzador titular de los Yankees desde el 1,74 de Ron Guidry en 1978.
Una votación que gira en torno a una definición
La historia pone de relieve lo que está en juego. Justin Verlander, en 2011, fue el último lanzador a tiempo completo en ganar el MVP de la Liga Americana, y Clayton Kershaw, en 2014, fue el último lanzador en ganarlo en cualquiera de las dos ligas. Ningún lanzador a tiempo completo de los Yankees ha conseguido el premio desde Spud Chandler en 1943.
Por eso este tira y afloja va más allá de un solo nombre. Rosenthal valora el rendimiento a través de los resultados. Cone lo valora a través de la ausencia. Ambos puntos de vista son defendibles, y ninguna votación resolverá cuál es el correcto.
Los Yankees, con la mirada puesta en octubre, preferirían que su as reservara lo mejor de sí mismo para la postemporada, independientemente de los trofeos. Pero, con una o dos salidas por delante, Schlittler todavía tiene margen para dar un empujoncito al debate. Por ahora, el tema sigue abierto, y un grande de los Yankees insiste en que la pregunta más antigua de este deporte aún merece una respuesta.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Aumenta El Temor A Que Aaron Judge Se Convierta En El Villano De Los Yankees En Octubre Tras Su último Contratiempo Por Lesión

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Durante más de tres meses, los Yankees de Nueva York han planificado el regreso de Aaron Judge en torno a una idea: recuperar a su capitán para octubre sin exigirle que recupere de golpe los 99 días que se ha perdido.
Por eso su primera semana tras el regreso nunca pareció normal. Judge volvió sin haber pasado por una etapa de rehabilitación en las ligas menores. Los Yankees limitaron sus entradas, intercalaron descansos programados y consideraron los partidos de las Grandes Ligas como la fase final de su preparación. Solo jugó seis entradas en su regreso el 8 de septiembre y el martes tuvo un descanso programado tras disputar seis partidos seguidos.
Los Yankees estaban dispuestos a sacrificar el ritmo de septiembre a cambio de la forma física en octubre. Para este fin de semana en Arizona, se suponía que esa ecuación iba a cambiar. Judge ya había superado la fase de entrenamiento controlado. Nueva York se preparaba para aumentar su carga de trabajo y darle esos turnos al bate regulares que se había perdido durante su larga recuperación en la liga mayor.
La urgencia ya se notaba en los resultados. Judge tenía un promedio de 4 de 21 con 11 strikeouts en sus primeros seis partidos tras su reincorporación. Su jonrón de tres carreras del lunes en Minnesota fue la primera señal de que estaba dando la talla, pero no borró todos esos swings fallidos. Los Yankees necesitaban más práctica que otro reinicio.
Según la clasificación de la MLB, los Yankees tienen un balance de 88-64 al comenzar el viernes, a cinco partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con 10 partidos por disputar. Cuatro de ellos serán contra los Rays la semana que viene. La plaza para la postemporada está asegurada, pero Nueva York todavía tiene que prepararse para la lucha por el título de división y una posible serie de comodines.
Por eso, esta etapa no se centró tanto en demostrar que Judge podía volver, sino más bien en asegurarse de que pudiera volver a asumir la carga de trabajo habitual de octubre. Se suponía que cada partido le acercaría un poco más a su máximo rendimiento, le ayudaría a recuperar la sincronización frente a los lanzadores de las Grandes Ligas y eliminaría otra incertidumbre de cara a la postemporada. Se suponía que esa iba a ser la fase final y sin complicaciones del plan de los Yankees para octubre, antes de que empezara la postemporada.
El plan de puesta en marcha se ve interrumpido
En cambio, Judge llega a Arizona con una molestia en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha tras la derrota del miércoles por 5-4, en la 13.ª entrada, ante los Minnesota Twins en el Target Field. Notó el problema por primera vez en la primera entrada y siguió en el campo hasta que Heliot Ramos entró como bateador suplente en su lugar en la sexta.
Era su séptimo partido desde que volvió tras una fractura por estrés en la costilla derecha, después de 99 días de baja. Con esos dos strikeouts, su promedio desde que volvió queda en 4 de 23, con 13 strikeouts y un jonrón.
Judge dijo que intentó seguir jugando antes de que él y el entrenador Aaron Boone decidieran que el riesgo para los Yankees era mayor que lo que valía seguir en el campo.
«Intenté seguir jugando a ver hasta dónde podía llegar, porque estos partidos son importantes en esta recta final», dijo Judge. «Lo hablé con los míos y pensamos que sería lo mejor para no perjudicar al equipo, ni en el campo ni en las bases».
Los Yankees tuvieron el jueves libre para someterse a tratamiento. A primera hora del viernes, la MLB seguía indicando que tenía una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha, sin fecha de regreso.
David Cone señala un problema aún mayor para octubre
La primera cuestión es la disponibilidad. La más importante es la preparación.
El analista de YES Network, David Cone, se centró en eso el jueves. Judge ha tenido 24 turnos al bate desde que volvió, y 13 de ellos han acabado en strikeouts.
«Estoy preocupado», dijo Cone. «Necesita turnos al bate… Tiene un problema en la parte inferior de la pierna, en la pantorrilla. Simplemente no lo sabemos. No lo sabremos hasta que sepamos qué tan grave es. ¿Va a tener más turnos al bate antes de que acabe la temporada regular? Ahora mismo es una auténtica incógnita».
Ahora, el hecho de haberse saltado la fase de rehabilitación cobra más importancia. El exreceptor All-Star A.J. Pierzynski dijo que una temporada en las ligas menores podría haberle proporcionado un entorno menos exigente para lidiar con las molestias tras una larga ausencia.
«Por eso te vas de rehabilitación, sobre todo cuando has estado tanto tiempo de baja como Aaron Judge. Él mismo lo ha dicho: esto es como los entrenamientos de primavera, así que intentas quitarte de encima las molestias y otras cosillas que surgen yendo de rehabilitación», dijo Pierzynski. «Él no lo hizo, no quiso hacerlo».
Nadie puede saber si una asignación a la rehabilitación habría evitado esa tensión en la pierna. Los Yankees ahora corren el riesgo de que Judge pierda más turnos al bate que aún necesita.
El equilibrio de los pelotones no es el problema
Una comparación actual del OPS de los Yankees y los Red Sox destaca a Judge, Ben Rice y Cody Bellinger como bateadores de Nueva York que rinden bien contra cualquiera de los dos equipos. Según Baseball Savant, Judge tiene un OPS de 0,839 contra lanzadores diestros y de 0,892 contra zurdos. Bellinger tiene unas cifras casi idénticas: 0,794 y 0,795. Rice tiene un OPS de 0,937 contra lanzadores diestros y de 0,784 contra zurdos.
Judge no necesita un papel de bateador de reserva. Los Yankees necesitan que esté listo para batear regularmente contra cualquier rival.
Judge tiene un promedio de bateo de .241/.360/.511, con 18 jonrones y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos. La cuestión es si los Yankees podrán recuperar el ritmo de juego suficiente antes de octubre.
El plazo de la Liga Internacional convierte la precaución en una apuesta con la plantilla
Si los Yankees metieran a Judge en la lista de lesionados ahora, no podría jugar hasta el partido 161, lo que le dejaría, como mucho, el último partido de la temporada regular para ponerse a punto.
Si los Yankees creen que puede volver antes, pueden mantenerlo en la plantilla y jugar temporalmente con un jugador menos disponible en la plantilla de 28.
Jasson Domínguez y Max Schuemann figuraban ambos en la alineación del equipo de Triple A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre el jueves, lo que sugiere que no habrá ningún sustituto inmediato.
Esto deja a Nueva York ante la disyuntiva que intentó evitar durante el primer regreso de Judge: proteger su físico o proteger su preparación. A falta de 10 partidos, puede que los Yankees no tengan tiempo suficiente para hacer ambas cosas a fondo.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
American sportscaster and host of a show on WFAN sports radio, Craig Carton, offered his blunt take on Yankees captain Aaron Judge calling the shots on his latest injury and playing time as October baseball approaches. Judge left the series finale against the Twins after just two at-bats because of minor stiffness in his lower right leg, prompting worried reactions from fans and clubhouse staff.
In his latest appearance on the radio show, Carton slammed Judge's reflection on the injury, his return to the active roster from the earlier 60-day IL, and how the Bombers captain hinted at not requiring extensive testing on the issue, as he believes it would quickly fix itself.
"They've said it to us on this show; well, Aaron Judge kind of will dictate when he comes back. He's not a doctor, he's not a P.T.I. expert… Yeah, but he doesn't own the franchise… The medical staff, the manager, and the general manager should decide… Just admit that you're not trying to win the division then, and I accept that. Because he's not ready to play at this level. He proved that. He was terrible," Carton said.
Watch the video here:
Judge hit a home run in Monday night's series opener against the Twins, but then had a routine day off on Tuesday. He was named to the starting lineup for Wednesday's game, but his early exit has been concerning for many, as the Bombers look destined to open their postseason with a Wild Card series against the Red Sox.
What Did Aaron Judge Say About His Early Exit From Wednesday's Game?
Speaking to the media after the game, Judge reflected on his injury, explaining that he chose not to aggravate it and spoke with the manager and medical staff about exiting the game as a precaution. Furthermore, the three-time AL MVP hoped he wouldn't need to undergo any testing, remaining optimistic that he could return to the field soon.
"We're still trying to ramp up, so there are going to be little things like this that come up. Just thought it would be best instead of pushing through it like I normally do… Once you start ramping up again, things pop up, and that's where we've been thankfully this whole time coming back. Nothing's really nagged us, so hopefully it's just one little thing and then we're back out there soon," Judge said.
The Yankees open a three-game series against the Diamondbacks at Chase Field on Friday, after which they head home for a crucial four-game series against the Tampa Bay Rays, whom they trail by five games in the AL East race with just 10 games remaining.

item.title: [Newsday] Yankees' Cam Schlittler would appear to be the front-runner for the American League Cy Young Award

item.content:encoded:
By any objective measure, Cam Schlittler, in his first full season in the majors, is having one of the best seasons any Yankees starter has ever had.
Schlittler, who is expected to start Saturday against the Diamondbacks in Phoenix, is 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA. Those numbers alone, however, don’t tell the full story of Schlittler’s 2026 season, one that has established him as a co-favorite, along with Dylan Cease of the Blue Jays, for the American League Cy Young Award.
After Schlittler threw six scoreless innings Sunday afternoon in a 2-0 victory over the Mets, manager Aaron Boone even made a push for him to be considered for another award.
“He might be the MVP, too,” Boone said. “It’s been awesome. Just an awesome season.”
That, of course, is a long shot at best. Many voters, not to mention players, see the MVP as the sole dominion of position players, just as the Cy Young Award is reserved for pitchers.
“He’s definitely pitching like an MVP,” Aaron Judge said after Sunday's win. “They’ve got a Cy Young Award for a reason — best pitcher in the game. He’s got my vote definitely for the Cy Young.”
Regardless, Schlittler is in the midst of a strong finishing kick to his year, and it is not a stretch to say he has emerged as the favorite with just over a week left in the regular season.
Though Schlittler has the edge over Cease in many of the numbers — traditional as well as what would be considered more “modern” ones — used when it comes to evaluating pitchers for the Cy Young Award, Cease has some of those in his favor as well.
Digging into many of those numbers, all of them as of Wednesday afternoon:
Schlittler is second in the American League in wins with 14 compared to 11 for Cease (11-6), though Cy Young Award voters have put little emphasis on wins in the last decade-plus.
The Mariners' Felix Hernandez, for instance, won the AL Cy Young Award in 2010 after going 13-12 (with an MLB-leading 2.27 ERA, one of many statistics, both old-school and new-school, in which he led). The Mets' Jacob deGrom won the NL award in 2018 after going 10-9 (with an MLB-best 1.70 ERA and dominating pretty much every other statistical category), and the Pirates' Paul Skenes took NL honors last season after going 10-10 (with an MLB-leading 1.97 ERA and widespread statistical dominance elsewhere).
Schlittler leads Cease in ERA, 1.95 to 2.38; walks and hits per innings pitched (WHIP), 0.90 to 1.06; innings, 184 2/3 to 166 1/3, and Wins above Replacement, 7.0 to 6.1, according to baseball-reference.com, and 5.9 to 5.6, according to Fangraphs.com.
Schlittler also holds the edge in ERA+, a statistic measuring the quality of a pitcher’s ERA compared to the league average, adjusting to the ballpark he pitches in, with the league average being 100.
Cease’s ERA+ is 185, a terrific, Cy Young Award-worthy number in many years, but this year it ranks him second in the AL to Schlittler’s extraordinary ERA+ of 216 (deGrom’s ERA+ in 2018 was 218, Skenes’ in 2025 was 226).
Schlittler's “calling card” from the time he was promoted to the big leagues in July 2025 has been command, according to Boone, and he dominates Cease in that category as well.
Despite pitching 18 1/3 more innings, Schlittler has walked only 44 batters to Cease's 72. Schlittler ranks fifth in the AL in walks per nine innings at 2.1 and Cease ranks 22nd at 3.9.
Cease does have some numbers in his favor.
Despite throwing 18 1/3 fewer innings, Cease has 236 strikeouts, tied for the MLB lead, to Schlittler’s 228, giving the former a ratio of 12.8 strikeouts per nine innings to the latter’s 11.1. Cease has 13 games with at least nine strikeouts, the most of any pitcher in the AL, and Schlittler has seven such games.
Cease has been slightly harder to hit, with opposing batters producing a .177 batting average against, which leads the AL among qualified starting pitchers, compared to a .185 batting average against for Schlittler (which ranks him second in that category). Cease is allowing 5.7 hits per nine innings and Schllittler is allowing 6.0.
Cease has allowed only 11 homers in his 166 1/3 innings and Schlittler has allowed 16 in his 184 2/3 innings.
Cease also holds the edge over Schlittler in Fielding Independent Pitching (FIP), which attempts to measure a pitcher’s performance based on those elements he directly controls before a ball is put in play and the vagaries of defense become a factor. Those would be strikeouts, walks, homers allowed and hit batsmen.
Cease leads the AL in FIP at 2.48. Schlittler is second at 2.57.
Though Cease does hold an advantage in some of the difficulty-to-hit categories, they likely won’t be enough — at the moment, anyway — to deny Schlittler's bid to become the seventh Yankee to win a Cy Young Award (Gerrit Cole was the most recent in 2023).
And there’s this: Schlittler’s closing argument has been especially eye-popping. He’s allowed one run or fewer in an MLB-leading (and franchise-record) 21 starts this season, including in each of his last seven starts, going 4-0 with a 1.00 ERA and a 0.76 WHIP in that span. He has a 0.81 ERA and 0.72 WHIP in those 21 games. In two other games, he allowed zero or one earned run.
Schlittler has allowed three or fewer runs in 27 of his 31 starts and two or fewer in 24 of them.
Cease has 16 outings in which he allowed one run or fewer, certainly an impressive number, but has not pitched quite as well of late, 4-0 with a 2.70 ERA in his previous seven outings.
